docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Vue.js] Web Framework

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude at the request of Serge Tahé - September 2026

This document is a translation of the original French version, generated using an automated tool. Some expressions or technical terms may not fully reflect the original meaning.

This course shows, step by step, how to write a web application with the Vue.js 3 framework: a single-page application (SPA) whose pages are built in the browser from the JSON data of a server.

It starts with 20 small examples, each focused on a single concept: a Vite project, reactivity (ref, reactive, computed, watch), directives, events, forms and their validation; components (props, events, v-model, slots, life cycle, composables, provide / inject); routing with vue-router, its parameters and navigation guards; shared state with Pinia stores; internationalization with vue-i18n; and finally talking to the server (fetch, Vite proxy, httpOnly cookie, API access layer, server errors).

The server is treated as a black box: it is the JSON server of the RdvMedecins application, written with NestJS. You install it, study its API and query it with 48 curl examples, without having to read its code.

Then comes a complete case study: the Vue.js client of RdvMedecins, an appointment-booking application for a medical practice, in which every file is commented, followed by its deployment.

This course follows the NestJS course, in which the server builds the pages. The same pages are written with other frameworks in the Angular, React and Flutter courses. The course A Vue.js/NestJS Client/Server Example studies both the server and the client.

All courses by Serge Tahé

docs.title: 13.1. Installation of Node.js
docs.text:
[Node.js] can be downloaded from nodejs.org: select version LTS (long-term support), preferably 22 ([Vite] 7 requires at least version 20.19). The [Windows] installer also installs [npm]. Verify the installation in a console:

node --version
npm --version

To run multiple versions of [Node.js] on the same machine, you can use [nvm-windows] (under [Windows]) or [nvm] (under [Linux] and [macOS]).

The examples and case study do not require the installation of any global tools: [Vite], [TypeScript], [vue-tsc] (and, for the server, the [nest] tool) are part of each project’s dependencies, installed by [npm install].

docs.title: 13.2. Installing Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
[Visual Studio Code] is downloaded via code.visualstudio.com. For the [.vue] files, install the Vue (Official) extension (publisher Vue.volar) from the Extensions panel (Ctrl+Shift+X): syntax highlighting, code completion, type checking ([TypeScript]) in templates, and navigation to the definition of a component or prop.

Open a project via the File / Open Folder menu (the [examples-vuejs] folder, for example), and open a console within it via the Terminal / New Terminal menu.

docs.title: 13.3. The Vue.js devtools extension
docs.text:
The Vue.js devtools extension can be installed from the extension store for [Chrome], [Edge], or [Firefox]. It adds a “Vue” tab to the browser’s developer tools (F12), which displays:

  • the page component tree, and, for each component, its props and state ([ref], [reactive], [computed]);
  • the [Pinia] stores and their contents;
  • the router's routes and the current route;
  • A timeline of events emitted by the components.

You can modify a piece of data there and watch the page update: an excellent way to understand reactivity.

docs.title: 13.4. Installing MySQL with Laragon
docs.text:
The JSON server requires [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]). [Laragon] (laragon.org) installs one under [Windows], ready to use, along with the [HeidiSQL] administration tool. After installation:

  • the “Start All” button launches the [MySQL] server on port 3306;
  • the user [root] has no password: these are the default values from the server’s [.env.example] file;
  • in [HeidiSQL] (the “Database” button), the File / Run SQL menu item runs the [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script.

In [Linux] or [macOS], install [MySQL] or [MariaDB] using the system’s package manager, and run the script using the command-line client: [mysql -u root -p < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql].

docs.title: 13.5. Installing curl
docs.text:
[curl] is included with [Windows] versions 10 and 11, [macOS], and most distributions of [Linux]. Check its version:

curl --version

The option [--json], used in this document, has been available since version 7.82 (2022). If you are using an older version, replace [--json @file] with [-H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @file], or install a recent version from curl.se.

In [PowerShell], you must enter [curl.exe], not [curl]: In [PowerShell], [curl] is an alias for another command ([Invoke-WebRequest]), which does not include the options from [curl]. The command prompt ([cmd]) does not have this issue.

docs.title: 10. Case Study: The Vue.js client for the RdvMedecins application
10.1. The Problem
docs.text:
The [RdvMedecins] application allows users to schedule appointments at a doctor’s office. The [NestJS] course wrote it as a HTML application, in which the server generated the pages. Here we are writing the client [Vue.js]: the SAME pages, generated in the browser from the JSON data on the server described in the chapter “The RdvMedecins Server: A Black Box.”

The client must provide everything that the HTML application provided:

  • a login page, protected by a CAPTCHA, with the option to create a patient account;
  • a doctor’s schedule for a given day, with appointment booking (patient selection window) and cancellation;
  • for the administrator, management of doctors and clients (list, add, edit, delete);
  • for the patient, a personal dashboard (showing upcoming appointments, which they can cancel) and account management;
  • two languages: French and English;
  • unique URLs ([/schedule?doctorId=1&day=...]), which can be reloaded, bookmarked, and navigated using the browser’s Back/Forward buttons.

docs.title: 10.2. Installation and Execution
docs.text:
The JSON server must be installed and running (see previous chapter). To use the client in a browser, you do not need the CAPTCHA test mode: you do NOT need to set it in the server’s [.env] file.

In a console window open to the [rdvmedecins-vuejs] folder:

npm install
npm run dev

Then open http://localhost:5173 in a browser. The demo accounts are listed on the login page (password = login).

The [Vite] server in the examples also uses port 5173. If this port is already in use, [Vite] will take another one (5174...) and display it in the console: you must then open that address.

docs.title: 10.5.2. vite.config.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// vite.config.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
//   - npm run dev   : development server on http://localhost:5173;
//                     the /api/... requests are forwarded to the JSON server
//                     (port 8080) by the proxy: page and API have the same
//                     origin, the token cookie travels normally;
//   - npm run build : the compiled application, in dist/. To put it in
//                     production, copy the CONTENT of dist/ into the
//                     client/ folder of the JSON server, which then serves it itself
//                     (see chapter "Deployment").
// =========================================================================

import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [vue()],
  server: {
    port: 5173,
    proxy: {
      '/api': 'http://localhost:8080',
    },
  },
  // npm run preview: serves dist/ (after npm run build), with the same proxy
  preview: {
    port: 4173,
    proxy: {
      '/api': 'http://localhost:8080',
    },
  },
});
  • lines 21–23: the proxy for requests from [/api] to the server JSON;
  • lines 26–31: the same proxy for [npm run preview].

An important detail: the application uses “clean” addresses ([/schedule], [/my-area]). If you reload the page [/schedule], the browser requests [/schedule] from the [Vite] server. Since the server cannot find a file with that name, it returns [index.html] (this is its default behavior for a single-page application); the application launches, and its router displays the calendar page.

  • line 18: without [JavaScript], a [Vue.js] application cannot display anything. The HTML application from the [NestJS] course, on the other hand, worked without [JavaScript]: that’s the trade-off of a single-page application;
  • Line 19: the program.

docs.title: 10.6.2. src/main.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// main.ts - the startup of the application
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
//   1. Bootstrap (CSS) and our few styles;
//   2. Pinia (stores), vue-i18n (languages), the router;
//   3. the reaction to a 401 response coming from any request:
//      the session has expired - we forget the user and go back to the
//      login page, with a message;
//   4. the display in <div id="app">.
// =========================================================================

import { createApp } from 'vue';
import { createPinia } from 'pinia';
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css';
import './styles.css';
import App from './App.vue';
import { i18n } from './i18n';
import { router } from './router';
import { whenUnauthenticated } from './api/http-client';
import { useSessionStore } from './stores/session';
import { useMessagesStore } from './stores/messages';

const app = createApp(App);
app.use(createPinia());
app.use(i18n);
app.use(router);

whenUnauthenticated(() => {
  useSessionStore().forget();
  useMessagesStore().flash('error', 'ERRORS.SESSION_EXPIRED');
  router.push({ name: 'login' });
});

app.mount('#app');
  • Lines 24–26: the three extensions: stores, languages, and the router. [Pinia] must be installed BEFORE the router: the router guard uses a store;
  • Lines 28–32: What to do when any request receives a 401 response (session expired, account deleted, etc.): forget the user, prepare the message “Your session has expired” for the next page, and redirect to the login page. This response is declared ONCE here; the function [whenUnauthenticated] is described with [http-client.ts].

docs.title: 10.6.3. src/App.vue
docs.text:
<!--
  =========================================================================
  App.vue - the root component: the TEMPLATE common to all the pages
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  The equivalent of views/layout.hbs of the HTML application:
    - the navigation bar;
    - a success message at the TOP;
    - the current page (<RouterView>);
    - the error panel at the BOTTOM;
    - the confirmation dialog, once for the whole application.

  :key="String(route.name)" on <RouterView>: when going from one route to
  ANOTHER (from /doctors to /clients, for example), the page component
  is recreated; when only the query changes (/schedule?day=...), it is
  kept, and it is the component that follows the URL.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { RouterView, useRoute } from 'vue-router';
import NavBar from './components/NavBar.vue';
import SuccessMessage from './components/SuccessMessage.vue';
import ErrorPanel from './components/ErrorPanel.vue';
import ConfirmDialog from './components/ConfirmDialog.vue';

const route = useRoute();
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4">
    <NavBar />
    <SuccessMessage />
    <RouterView :key="String(route.name)" />
    <ErrorPanel />
  </div>
  <ConfirmDialog />
</template>

The template common to all pages, equivalent to [views/layout.hbs]:

  • line 30: the navigation bar;
  • line 31: a success message at the top;
  • line 32: the current page. The [:key] attribute: when a component’s key changes, [Vue.js] destroys it and creates a new one. With the route NAME as the key, switching from [/doctors] to [/clients] (two different routes, displayed by the same component) recreates the page, which reloads its data. When only the [query] changes (to [/schedule?day=...]), the page is retained, and it is this page that follows its URL;
  • line 33: the error area, at the bottom;
  • line 35: the confirmation window, displayed once for the entire application.

docs.title: 10.7.1. src/api/types.ts
docs.text:
The JSON objects of the API, described in the chapter on the black box, translated into [TypeScript] interfaces:

// =========================================================================
// api/types.ts - the JSON objects exchanged with the server
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The translation, into TypeScript interfaces, of the API described in the chapter
// "The server, a black box". The compiler thus checks that the client
// only uses fields that really exist.
// =========================================================================

export type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'DOCTOR' | 'USER';

// POST /api/auth/login, GET /api/auth/me, PUT /api/my-account
export interface User {
  login: string;
  name: string; // display name: "Marie PELISSIER"
  role: Role;
}

// GET /api/captcha
export interface Captcha {
  id: string;
  svg: string;
}

// a title, a first name, a last name
export interface Identity {
  title: string;
  firstName: string;
  lastName: string;
}

// a doctor or a client: GET /api/doctors, GET /api/clients/:id...
export interface Person extends Identity {
  id: number;
  version: number; // optimistic lock: to send back with an update
  login?: string; // only for the ADMIN
}

// what is sent to create / update a person (ADMIN)
export interface PersonData extends Identity {
  login: string; // '' = default value (creation) or unchanged (update)
  password: string; // same
  version?: number;
}

export interface Slot {
  id: number;
  startHour: number;
  startMinute: number;
  endHour: number;
  endMinute: number;
}

// a row of the schedule, with the RIGHTS of the logged-in user
export interface ScheduleSlot extends Slot {
  free: boolean;
  patient: Identity | null; // null: free, or taken by another patient
  mine: boolean; // the appointment of the logged-in patient
  bookable: boolean;
  appointmentId: number | null; // filled in if the user can cancel
}

// GET /api/schedule?doctorId=...&day=...
export interface Schedule {
  doctor: Person;
  day: string; // "yyyy-MM-dd"
  slots: ScheduleSlot[];
  info: string | null; // translation key (patient who already has an appointment)
}

// GET /api/my-area
export interface MyArea {
  patient: Identity;
  appointments: { id: number; day: string; slot: Slot; doctor: Person }[];
}

// GET /api/my-account
export interface MyAccount extends Identity {
  login: string;
  version: number;
}

// PUT /api/my-account
export interface MyAccountUpdate extends Identity {
  login: string;
  password: string; // '' = unchanged
  confirmation: string;
  currentPassword: string;
  version: number;
}

// POST /api/register
export interface Registration extends Identity {
  login: string;
  password: string;
  confirmation: string;
}
  • line 32: one interface can extend another: a [Person] is an [Identity] that additionally has an ID, a version, and, for the ADMIN, a login;
  • Line 54: An entry in the calendar: a time slot, plus the permissions of the logged-in user;
  • lines 39 and following: what the client SENDS to the server.

docs.title: 10.7.2. src/api/http-client.ts
docs.text:
The [request] function from Example 19 ([common/api.ts]), with centralized handling of the 401 response:

// =========================================================================
// api/http-client.ts - the function that sends ALL the requests to the API
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Taken from common/api.ts of the examples, with one new feature: the
// centralized handling of the 401 response.
//
// A 401 can happen at any time: the token has expired (2 hours), the
// account has been deleted, the server has restarted with another secret
// key... Rather than handling this case in each component, we
// notify ONE function, registered at startup (see main.ts), which forgets
// the user and sends back to the login page.
// =========================================================================

export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(
    public readonly statusCode: number, // 0: the server did not respond
    public readonly key: string, // translation key: 'ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN'
    public readonly params: Record<string, string> = {},
    public readonly fields: Record<string, string> = {}, // error of each field
  ) {
    super(key);
    this.name = 'ApiError';
  }
}

// the function called on each 401 response (see main.ts)
let onUnauthenticated: (error: ApiError) => void = () => {};

export function whenUnauthenticated(callback: (error: ApiError) => void): void {
  onUnauthenticated = callback;
}

type Method = 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE';

export interface RequestOptions {
  // the public routes (login, captcha...) and GET /api/auth/me
  // handle the 401 themselves: no automatic redirect
  ignore401?: boolean;
}

export async function request<T>(method: Method, url: string, body?: unknown, options: RequestOptions = {}): Promise<T> {
  let response: Response;
  try {
    response = await fetch(`/api${url}`, {
      method,
      headers: body !== undefined ? { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Accept: 'application/json' } : { Accept: 'application/json' },
      body: body !== undefined ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
    });
  } catch {
    throw new ApiError(0, 'ERRORS.SERVER_UNREACHABLE');
  }

  // read as text then converted: an empty response, or one that is not
  // JSON (server stopped: it is the Vite proxy that answers), does not
  // crash the application
  const text = await response.text();
  let data: unknown = null;
  try {
    data = text ? JSON.parse(text) : null;
  } catch {
    data = null;
  }

  if (response.ok) {
    return data as T;
  }

  const e = (data ?? {}) as { key?: string; params?: Record<string, string>; fields?: Record<string, string> };
  const error = new ApiError(
    response.status,
    // no key: it is not our server that answered, but a proxy
    // (Vite: 500 without a body; nginx: 502, 504...)
    e.key ?? (response.status >= 500 ? 'ERRORS.SERVER_UNREACHABLE' : 'ERRORS.SERVER_ERROR'),
    e.params,
    e.fields,
  );
  if (response.status === 401 && !options.ignore401) {
    onUnauthenticated(error);
  }
  throw error;
}
  • lines 14–23: a request error: HTTP code, message key, parameters, error for each field;
  • line 27: the function to be called for each 401 response. It does nothing initially; [main.ts] provides one, via [whenUnauthenticated]. Why not call the router directly here? Because the API access layer should know nothing about the pages: it signals the error, and the application decides;
  • lines 35–39: some requests expect a 401 and handle it themselves: an incorrect password ([POST /api/auth/login] responds with a 401), or the question “who is logged in?” ([GET /api/auth/me], 401 if no one is logged in). For these, there is no automatic redirection;
  • Line 46: The header [Accept] tells the server the desired response format;
  • line 50: no response at all;
  • line 73: a response without a key does not come from our server: when the JSON server is down, the proxy responds (the one for [Vite] returns a 500 error with no body; a production proxy like [nginx] returns a 502 or 504);

docs.title: 10.7.3. src/api/rdvmedecins.api.ts
docs.text:
A function per API route:

// =========================================================================
// api/rdvmedecins.api.ts - one function per route of the API
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The "data access layer" of the client: the components call these
// typed functions, without knowing anything about URLs, fetch or JSON. If the API
// changes, only this file changes.
// =========================================================================

import { request } from './http-client';
import type {
  Schedule,
  Captcha,
  PersonData,
  Registration,
  MyAccountUpdate,
  MyAccount,
  MyArea,
  Person,
  User,
} from './types';

// /api/doctors or /api/clients: both are managed in the same way
export type PersonType = 'doctors' | 'clients';

type Empty = Record<string, never>;

export const rdvApi = {
  // ------------------------------------------------ login (public routes)
  captcha: () => request<Captcha>('GET', '/captcha', undefined, { ignore401: true }),
  me: () => request<User>('GET', '/auth/me', undefined, { ignore401: true }),
  logIn: (login: string, password: string, captchaId: string, captcha: string) =>
    request<User>('POST', '/auth/login', { login, password, captchaId, captcha }, { ignore401: true }),
  logOut: () => request<Empty>('POST', '/auth/logout', {}, { ignore401: true }),

  // ------------------------------------------------ account creation (public)
  registrationAccess: (captchaId: string, captcha: string) =>
    request<Empty>('POST', '/register/access', { captchaId, captcha }, { ignore401: true }),
  registrationAccessStatus: () => request<{ valid: boolean }>('GET', '/register/access', undefined, { ignore401: true }),
  register: (data: Registration) => request<{ login: string }>('POST', '/register', data, { ignore401: true }),

  // ------------------------------------------------ schedule and appointments
  // doctorId null: for a logged-in doctor, THEIR schedule
  schedule: (doctorId: number | null, day: string) => {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({ day });
    if (doctorId !== null) {
      params.set('doctorId', String(doctorId));
    }
    return request<Schedule>('GET', `/schedule?${params}`);
  },
  book: (day: string, slotId: number, clientId: number | null) =>
    request<{ id: number }>('POST', '/appointments', { day, slotId, clientId: clientId ?? undefined }),
  cancelAppointment: (appointmentId: number) => request<Empty>('DELETE', `/appointments/${appointmentId}`),

  // ------------------------------------------------ doctors and clients
  list: (type: PersonType) => request<Person[]>('GET', `/${type}`),
  read: (type: PersonType, id: number) => request<Person>('GET', `/${type}/${id}`),
  add: (type: PersonType, data: PersonData) => request<Person>('POST', `/${type}`, data),
  edit: (type: PersonType, id: number, data: PersonData) =>
    request<Person>('PUT', `/${type}/${id}`, data),
  remove: (type: PersonType, id: number) => request<Empty>('DELETE', `/${type}/${id}`),

  // ------------------------------------------------ the patient's area
  myArea: () => request<MyArea>('GET', '/my-area'),
  myAccount: () => request<MyAccount>('GET', '/my-account'),
  editMyAccount: (data: MyAccountUpdate) => request<User>('PUT', '/my-account', data),
  deleteMyAccount: (currentPassword: string) => request<Empty>('DELETE', '/my-account', { currentPassword }),
};
  • line 23: doctors and clients are handled the same way; only the address changes: [/api/doctors] or [/api/clients];
  • line 25: the type of an empty object, [{}];
  • Lines 29–33: the connection routes, which handle their own 401 ([ignore401]);
  • lines 43–49: if no doctor is available, the parameter [doctorId] is omitted; if a doctor is available, the server returns THEIR schedule;
  • lines 50–51: [clientId ?? undefined]: [null] becomes [undefined], and [JSON.stringify] omits the properties of [undefined]: a patient does not send [clientId];
  • lines 55–60: the five operations on individuals, defined by their type;
  • line 66: a DELETE query can also have a body.

docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// i18n.ts - French and English
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The locales/fr.json and locales/en.json dictionaries are those of the
// NestJS course (i18n/*.json), completed with a few keys specific to the client
// (ERRORS.SERVER_UNREACHABLE...). The JSON server only returns KEYS
// ('ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN'): they are the same as those of the dictionaries.
//
// The chosen language is stored in localStorage (a preference, not
// sensitive data); failing that, the browser's language is used.
// =========================================================================

import { createI18n } from 'vue-i18n';
import fr from './locales/fr.json';
import en from './locales/en.json';

export type Language = 'fr' | 'en';
export const LANGUAGES: Language[] = ['fr', 'en'];
const STORAGE_KEY = 'rdvmedecins.language';

function initialLanguage(): Language {
  try {
    const stored = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY);
    if (stored === 'fr' || stored === 'en') {
      return stored;
    }
  } catch {
    // localStorage unavailable (strict private browsing...): never mind
  }
  return navigator.language.toLowerCase().startsWith('fr') ? 'fr' : 'en';
}

export const i18n = createI18n({
  legacy: false,
  locale: initialLanguage(),
  fallbackLocale: 'en',
  messages: { fr, en },
  // no warning in the console for a key translated by fallback
  fallbackWarn: false,
  missingWarn: false,
});

// change the language: the whole application is translated again at once
export function changeLanguage(language: Language): void {
  i18n.global.locale.value = language;
  document.documentElement.lang = language;
  try {
    localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, language);
  } catch {
    // of no importance
  }
}

document.documentElement.lang = i18n.global.locale.value;
  • lines 21–31: the stored language, otherwise the browser’s language. Access to [localStorage] is protected by [try / catch]: some browsers, in incognito mode, block it;
  • lines 39–40: no warning in the console when a key is missing or comes from the fallback dictionary;
  • lines 44–52: change language: [i18n.global.locale] is the language for the entire application; the page’s [lang] attribute is also updated, and the selection is saved.

docs.title: 10.9.1. src/stores/session.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// stores/session.ts - WHO is logged in?
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The Pinia store of the session: the logged-in user (or null), and what
// is deduced from it (is the user an ADMIN? a patient?).
//
// The JWT token itself is NOT here: it is in an httpOnly cookie that
// only the browser handles. The store keeps only the DESCRIPTION of
// the user, returned by the server ({ login, name, role }).
//
// At startup (and after an F5), the store is empty: check() asks the
// server, only once, who is logged in (GET /api/auth/me).
// =========================================================================

import { computed, ref } from 'vue';
import { defineStore } from 'pinia';
import { rdvApi } from '../api/rdvmedecins.api';
import type { Role, User } from '../api/types';

export const useSessionStore = defineStore('session', () => {
  const user = ref<User | null>(null);
  // has the question "who is logged in?" already been asked to the server?
  let checking: Promise<void> | null = null;

  const loggedIn = computed(() => user.value !== null);
  const role = computed<Role | null>(() => user.value?.role ?? null);
  const isAdmin = computed(() => role.value === 'ADMIN');
  const isPatient = computed(() => role.value === 'USER');
  // ADMIN and DOCTOR: book and cancel the appointments of any patient
  const isManager = computed(() => role.value === 'ADMIN' || role.value === 'DOCTOR');

  // the home page of each role, right after login
  const homePage = computed(() => (isPatient.value ? '/my-area' : '/schedule'));

  // called by the router guard before EACH navigation; only queries
  // the server the first time (the promise is kept and reused)
  function check(): Promise<void> {
    checking ??= rdvApi
      .me()
      .then((u) => {
        user.value = u;
      })
      .catch(() => {
        user.value = null; // 401: nobody; or server unreachable
      });
    return checking;
  }

  async function logIn(login: string, password: string, captchaId: string, captcha: string): Promise<void> {
    user.value = await rdvApi.logIn(login, password, captchaId, captcha);
  }

  // the user has changed name or login (PUT /api/my-account)
  function update(u: User): void {
    user.value = u;
  }

  async function logOut(): Promise<void> {
    try {
      await rdvApi.logOut();
    } finally {
      forget();
    }
  }

  // without asking the server anything: session expired, account deleted
  function forget(): void {
    user.value = null;
  }

  return {
    user,
    loggedIn,
    role,
    isAdmin,
    isPatient,
    isManager,
    homePage,
    check,
    logIn,
    update,
    logOut,
    forget,
  };
});
  • Line 21: the logged-in user, as described by the server. The token itself isn’t there—it’s in a cookie that only the browser handles;
  • lines 25–30: what is inferred from this, used by the pages and the navigation bar;
  • line 33: the home page for each role: “My area” for a patient, the calendar for others;
  • lines 37–47: the question “Who is logged in?”, asked of the server only the FIRST time. The promise is kept in [checking]: subsequent calls reuse it (the operator [??=] only assigns a value if the variable is [null] or [undefined]). It cannot fail: an error (401, server unreachable) means “no one”;
  • lines 49–51: the login. If it fails, [rdvApi.logIn] rejects its promise with a [ApiError], which passes through this function to the login page;
  • line 54: After making changes to their account, the patient may have changed their name;
  • lines 58–64: [finally]: the user is forgotten, even if the server did not respond;
  • line 67: without making any request to the server (session expired, account deleted).

docs.title: 10.9.2. src/stores/messages.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// stores/messages.ts - the messages displayed to the user
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Same presentation as the HTML application:
//   - a SUCCESS is displayed at the TOP of the page (green banner);
//   - an ERROR at the BOTTOM, on a light pink background ("sticky" panel).
// A message is a translation KEY (+ its parameters): it is therefore
// translated again on its own if the user changes the language.
//
// The "flash" messages: an action that ends with a change of
// page (booking, adding a doctor...) leaves its message with flash();
// it will be displayed on the NEXT page, then disappear at the following
// navigation (see router.afterEach in router.ts). On the server side, it was the
// role of the short-lived "rdvmedecins_flash" cookie.
// =========================================================================

import { ref } from 'vue';
import { defineStore } from 'pinia';
import { ApiError } from '../api/http-client';

export interface Message {
  key: string;
  params?: Record<string, string>;
}

export const useMessagesStore = defineStore('messages', () => {
  const success = ref<Message | null>(null);
  const error = ref<Message | null>(null);
  // the messages to display on the next page
  let pending: { success: Message | null; error: Message | null } | null = null;

  function showSuccess(key: string, params?: Record<string, string>): void {
    success.value = { key, params };
    error.value = null;
  }

  function showError(key: string, params?: Record<string, string>): void {
    error.value = { key, params };
    success.value = null;
  }

  // an ApiError -> the message of the page; any other error is an
  // anomaly of the client, which is let through (browser console)
  function showApiError(e: unknown): void {
    if (!(e instanceof ApiError)) {
      throw e;
    }
    showError(e.key, e.params);
  }

  function clear(): void {
    success.value = null;
    error.value = null;
  }

  // for the NEXT page
  function flash(type: 'success' | 'error', key: string, params?: Record<string, string>): void {
    pending ??= { success: null, error: null };
    pending[type] = { key, params };
  }

  // called after each navigation (router.afterEach)
  function newPage(): void {
    success.value = pending?.success ?? null;
    error.value = pending?.error ?? null;
    pending = null;
  }

  return { success, error, showSuccess, showError, showApiError, clear, flash, newPage };
});
  • lines 21–24: A message consists of a translation KEY and its parameters. It therefore automatically translates itself if the user changes languages;
  • lines 27–28: the success message (displayed at the top) and the error message (at the bottom) for the current page;
  • lines 44–49: a [ApiError] becomes the page’s message. Any other error is a CLIENT anomaly (a programming error): it is allowed to be logged and will be displayed in the browser console;
  • lines 57–60: a message for the NEXT page. An action that results in a page change (booking, adding a doctor, logging in after creating an account) displays this message before navigating to the next page;
  • lines 63–67: called after each page navigation (see [router.ts]): messages from the previous page disappear, and pending messages appear. In the HTML application, this was the role of the short-lived cookie [rdvmedecins_flash].

docs.title: 10.10.1. src/composables/useConfirmation.ts
docs.text:
The composable from Example 12, with three differences:

// =========================================================================
// composables/useConfirmation.ts - "Are you sure?"
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Taken from example 12: confirm(key) opens the confirmation dialog
// (components/ConfirmDialog.vue, placed once in App.vue) and
// returns a promise resolved to true (Yes) or false (No). The message is
// a translation KEY: the dialog translates it into the current language.
//
//     if (await confirm('SCHEDULE.CANCEL_CONFIRM')) { ... }
// =========================================================================

import { readonly, ref } from 'vue';
import { useMessagesStore } from '../stores/messages';

const messageKey = ref<string | null>(null); // null: dialog closed
let answer: ((yes: boolean) => void) | null = null;

export function useConfirmation() {
  function confirm(key: string): Promise<boolean> {
    answer?.(false); // a question still open? it counts as "no"
    // a new question: the messages of the previous action are outdated
    useMessagesStore().clear();
    messageKey.value = key;
    return new Promise<boolean>((resolve) => {
      answer = resolve;
    });
  }

  function respond(yes: boolean): void {
    messageKey.value = null;
    const r = answer;
    answer = null;
    r?.(yes);
  }

  return { messageKey: readonly(messageKey), confirm, respond };
}
  • line 19: the message is a translation KEY: the window translates it into the current language;
  • line 20: an open question (unlikely scenario) receives the answer “no”;
  • line 22: a new question renders the messages from the previous action obsolete.

docs.title: 10.10.2. src/composables/useFormatting.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// composables/useFormatting.ts - the display of persons, times and days
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The server sends RAW data (startHour: 8, startMinute: 0; day:
// "2026-10-05"); the formatting, which depends on the language, is the business
// of the client. longDate() follows the current language of vue-i18n.
// =========================================================================

import { useI18n } from 'vue-i18n';
import type { Slot, Identity } from '../api/types';

// "Mme Alice DURAND"
export function label(p: Identity): string {
  return `${p.title} ${p.firstName} ${p.lastName}`;
}

// "8:05" rather than "8:5"
export function time(h: number, m: number): string {
  return `${h}:${String(m).padStart(2, '0')}`;
}

// "8:00 - 8:20"
export function timeRange(s: Slot): string {
  return `${time(s.startHour, s.startMinute)} - ${time(s.endHour, s.endMinute)}`;
}

// today's date, in the "yyyy-MM-dd" format (that of <input type="date"> and of the API)
export function today(): string {
  const d = new Date();
  return `${d.getFullYear()}-${String(d.getMonth() + 1).padStart(2, '0')}-${String(d.getDate()).padStart(2, '0')}`;
}

// true if [day] is a date that exists in the yyyy-MM-dd format
export function isValidDate(day: unknown): day is string {
  if (typeof day !== 'string' || !/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(day)) {
    return false;
  }
  const date = new Date(`${day}T00:00:00Z`);
  return !isNaN(date.getTime()) && date.toISOString().slice(0, 10) === day;
}

export function useFormatting() {
  const { locale } = useI18n();

  // "lundi 5 octobre 2026" / "Monday 5 October 2026"
  function longDate(day: string): string {
    return new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale.value === 'en' ? 'en-GB' : 'fr-FR', {
      dateStyle: 'full',
      timeZone: 'UTC', // "2026-10-05T00:00:00Z" must remain the 5th, whatever the time zone
    }).format(new Date(`${day}T00:00:00Z`));
  }

  return { label, time, timeRange, longDate };
}

The server sends raw data ([startHour: 8, startMinute: 0], [day: "2026-10-05"]); formatting this data, which depends on the language, is the client’s responsibility:

  • lines 13–39: ordinary, non-reactive functions, exported one by one;
  • lines 42–54: a composable, because [longDate] requires the CURRENT language, which it obtains via [useI18n()]. When the language changes, a template that displays [longDate(...)] is recalculated;
  • line 49: [new Date("2026-10-05T00:00:00Z")] is midnight UTC; displayed in the Paris time zone, it would still be October 5, but in New York, it would be October 4! We therefore request a display in the UTC time zone.

docs.title: 10.10.3. src/composables/useForm.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// composables/useForm.ts - the errors of a form sent to the server
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// All the forms of the application follow the same pattern as
// example 20: no rule is checked in the browser (they
// live in ONE single place, the server), and on refusal:
//   - the error of each field (ApiError.fields) is displayed under the field,
//     outlined in red;
//   - the general message (ApiError.key) is displayed at the bottom of the page.
// This composable groups this state and these actions.
// =========================================================================

import { ref } from 'vue';
import { ApiError } from '../api/http-client';
import { useMessagesStore } from '../stores/messages';

export function useForm() {
  const messages = useMessagesStore();
  const errors = ref<Record<string, string>>({}); // field -> message key
  const params = ref<Record<string, string>>({}); // parameters of the messages ({min}...)
  const submitting = ref(false);

  function clearErrors(): void {
    errors.value = {};
    params.value = {};
  }

  // runs the submission; returns true if it succeeded. On an ApiError, the
  // errors are displayed and false is returned.
  async function submit(action: () => Promise<void>): Promise<boolean> {
    clearErrors();
    submitting.value = true;
    try {
      await action();
      return true;
    } catch (e) {
      if (e instanceof ApiError) {
        errors.value = e.fields;
        params.value = e.params;
      }
      messages.showApiError(e);
      return false;
    } finally {
      submitting.value = false;
    }
  }

  return { errors, params, submitting, submit, clearErrors };
}

All forms in the application follow the approach shown in Example 20: no rules are validated in the browser; the server validates everything, and any errors are displayed below the fields. This composable groups together the state and common actions:

  • lines 19–21: the error for each field, the message parameters, and a submission indicator (the button is disabled during submission to prevent double-clicking);
  • lines 30–46: executes the submission (a function provided by the page); if [ApiError] occurs, clears the field errors, displays the general message at the bottom of the page, and returns [false].

docs.title: 10.11. The router
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// router.ts - the pages of the application and their access rights
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The SAME addresses as the HTML application (/login, /schedule, /doctors,
// /my-area...), but they are now routes of the CLIENT:
// createWebHistory produces "clean" addresses, without #. The browser
// sends a request to the server only for the very first page; after that,
// the router changes the address and the displayed component.
//
// The other side of the coin: if the user reloads /schedule (F5), the
// browser really does request /schedule from the server, which must then
// send back index.html (Vite does it in development; in production, see
// web/client-spa.ts of the JSON server).
//
// Each route carries metadata (meta):
//   - title   : translation key of the tab title;
//   - public  : accessible without being logged in;
//   - roles   : the allowed roles (absent = all logged-in roles);
//   - type    : 'doctors' or 'clients' for the pages common to both.
//
// REMINDER: these checks are only a CONVENIENCE (not displaying a useless
// page). The data is protected by the server, which
// checks the token and the role again on EACH request.
// =========================================================================

import { createRouter, createWebHistory } from 'vue-router';
import type { Role } from './api/types';
import type { PersonType } from './api/rdvmedecins.api';
import { i18n } from './i18n';
import { useSessionStore } from './stores/session';
import { useMessagesStore } from './stores/messages';
import { rdvApi } from './api/rdvmedecins.api';
import LoginView from './views/LoginView.vue';
import ScheduleView from './views/ScheduleView.vue';

declare module 'vue-router' {
  interface RouteMeta {
    title: string;
    public?: boolean;
    roles?: Role[];
    type?: PersonType;
  }
}

// the routes to manage doctors AND clients (ADMIN), on the same model
function personRoutes(type: PersonType, title: string, addTitle: string, editTitle: string) {
  const roles: Role[] = ['ADMIN'];
  return [
    { path: `/${type}`, name: type, component: () => import('./views/PersonsView.vue'), meta: { title, roles, type } },
    {
      path: `/${type}/add`,
      name: `${type}-add`,
      component: () => import('./views/PersonFormView.vue'),
      meta: { title: addTitle, roles, type },
    },
    {
      path: `/${type}/:id(\\d+)/edit`, // (\\d+): the id must be a number
      name: `${type}-edit`,
      component: () => import('./views/PersonFormView.vue'),
      props: (route: { params: { id?: string | string[] } }) => ({ id: Number(route.params.id) }),
      meta: { title: editTitle, roles, type },
    },
  ];
}

export const router = createRouter({
  history: createWebHistory(),
  routes: [
    // "/": to /login, which itself sends to the role's home page if logged in
    { path: '/', redirect: '/login' },
    { path: '/login', name: 'login', component: LoginView, meta: { title: 'LOGIN.TITLE', public: true } },
    { path: '/schedule', name: 'schedule', component: ScheduleView, meta: { title: 'SCHEDULE.PAGE_TITLE' } },
    ...personRoutes('doctors', 'DOCTORS.TITLE', 'DOCTORS.ADD', 'DOCTORS.EDIT'),
    ...personRoutes('clients', 'CLIENTS.TITLE', 'CLIENTS.ADD', 'CLIENTS.EDIT'),
    {
      path: '/register',
      name: 'register',
      component: () => import('./views/RegisterView.vue'),
      meta: { title: 'REGISTRATION.TITLE', public: true },
      // a guard SPECIFIC to the route: without a pass (captcha solved on the
      // login page), back to the login page
      beforeEnter: async () => {
        const { valid } = await rdvApi.registrationAccessStatus().catch(() => ({ valid: false }));
        if (!valid) {
          useMessagesStore().flash('error', 'ERRORS.CAPTCHA_BEFORE_ACCOUNT');
          return { name: 'login' };
        }
        return true;
      },
    },
    {
      path: '/my-area',
      name: 'my-area',
      component: () => import('./views/PatientAreaView.vue'),
      meta: { title: 'AREA.TITLE', roles: ['USER'] },
    },
    {
      path: '/my-account',
      name: 'my-account',
      component: () => import('./views/MyAccountView.vue'),
      meta: { title: 'MY_ACCOUNT.TITLE', roles: ['USER'] },
    },
    {
      path: '/forbidden',
      name: 'forbidden',
      component: () => import('./views/ErrorView.vue'),
      props: { code: 403 },
      meta: { title: 'ERROR_PAGE.TITLE' },
    },
    {
      path: '/:pathMatch(.*)*',
      name: 'not-found',
      component: () => import('./views/ErrorView.vue'),
      props: { code: 404 },
      meta: { title: 'ERROR_PAGE.TITLE', public: true },
    },
  ],
});

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// the GLOBAL guard, before each navigation
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
router.beforeEach(async (to) => {
  const session = useSessionStore();
  // the first time (startup, F5): we ask the server who is logged in
  await session.check();

  if (to.meta.public) {
    // already logged in: the login page no longer makes sense
    if (to.name === 'login' && session.loggedIn) {
      return session.homePage;
    }
    return true;
  }
  if (!session.loggedIn) {
    // the requested page is remembered, to come back to it after login
    return { name: 'login', query: { redirect: to.fullPath } };
  }
  if (to.meta.roles && !to.meta.roles.includes(session.role!)) {
    return { name: 'forbidden' };
  }
  return true;
});

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// after each navigation: "flash" messages, tab title
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
router.afterEach((to, from) => {
  // a navigation that changes only the query (/schedule?...) is still a
  // new "page": as with the HTML application, the messages of the
  // previous page disappear, the flash messages appear
  if (to.fullPath !== from.fullPath) {
    useMessagesStore().newPage();
  }
  document.title = `${i18n.global.t(to.meta.title)} - ${i18n.global.t('APP.TITLE')}`;
});
  • lines 36–43: metadata for our routes: the tab title (a translation key), public access, authorized roles, and user type;
  • Lines 46–64: the three doctor management routes (list, add, edit), and the same three for clients, generated by a function. The pages are loaded on demand ([() => import(...)]): a patient will never download the doctor management code;
  • Line 57: [(\d+)]: A regular expression restricts the parameter [id] to numbers. [/doctors/abc/edit] does not match this route: the “page not found” page is displayed;
  • line 60: the component’s [id] property, converted to a number;
  • line 67: “clean” addresses, without [#];
  • line 70: the address [/] leads to [/login], which in turn leads to the role’s home page when logged in;
  • lines 82–89: a guard SPECIFIC to a route, executed before entering it: without a pass (captcha solved on the login page), account creation redirects to the login page with a message;
  • line 107: [props] can also be a static object: the same error page is used for 403 and 404 errors;
  • Lines 123–143: The GLOBAL guard, before each navigation:
    • [await session.check()]: The first time (on startup, F5), the server is queried to determine who is logged in. The guard is [async]: navigation waits for the response;
    • a public page is always accessible; however, the login page, for a logged-in user, redirects to their home page;
    • not logged in: login page, while retaining the requested page;
    • invalid role: 403 page;
  • lines 148–156: after each navigation: the messages flash, and the tab title is translated. [i18n.global.t]: outside a component, the [i18n] object is used directly.

<!--
  =========================================================================
  components/NavBar.vue - the navigation bar
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Same content as that of the HTML application (views/partials/navbar.hbs):
  title, menus according to the role, FR / EN, role, name, logout.
  "Doctors" and "Patients" appear only for the ADMIN: a mere display
  convenience, the real protection being that of the server.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { RouterLink, useRouter } from 'vue-router';
import { useI18n } from 'vue-i18n';
import { useSessionStore } from '../stores/session';
import { changeLanguage, LANGUAGES } from '../i18n';

const { t, locale } = useI18n();
const session = useSessionStore();
const router = useRouter();

async function logOut(): Promise<void> {
  await session.logOut().catch(() => {}); // even if the server does not respond
  router.push({ name: 'login' });
}
</script>

<template>
  <nav class="navbar navbar-expand-sm navbar-dark bg-primary rounded mb-4 px-3">
    <span class="navbar-brand mb-0">{{ t('APP.TITLE') }}</span>

    <ul v-if="session.loggedIn" class="navbar-nav me-auto">
      <li v-if="session.isPatient" class="nav-item">
        <!-- active-class: the Bootstrap class of the menu of the displayed page -->
        <RouterLink class="nav-link" active-class="active" to="/my-area">{{ t('APP.MENU_MY_AREA') }}</RouterLink>
      </li>
      <li class="nav-item">
        <RouterLink class="nav-link" active-class="active" to="/schedule">{{ t('APP.MENU_SCHEDULE') }}</RouterLink>
      </li>
      <template v-if="session.isAdmin">
        <li class="nav-item">
          <RouterLink class="nav-link" active-class="active" to="/doctors">{{ t('APP.MENU_DOCTORS') }}</RouterLink>
        </li>
        <li class="nav-item">
          <RouterLink class="nav-link" active-class="active" to="/clients">{{ t('APP.MENU_PATIENTS') }}</RouterLink>
        </li>
      </template>
    </ul>
    <div v-else class="me-auto"></div>

    <div class="d-flex align-items-center gap-2">
      <!-- FR / EN: no request to the server, the page is translated again in place -->
      <div class="btn-group btn-group-sm" role="group" :aria-label="t('APP.LANGUAGE')">
        <button
          v-for="l in LANGUAGES"
          :key="l"
          type="button"
          class="btn"
          :class="locale === l ? 'btn-light' : 'btn-outline-light'"
          :aria-pressed="locale === l"
          @click="changeLanguage(l)"
        >
          {{ l.toUpperCase() }}
        </button>
      </div>

      <template v-if="session.user">
        <span class="badge text-bg-light text-primary">{{ session.user.role }}</span>
        <span class="text-white">{{ session.user.name }}</span>
        <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-light" @click="logOut">{{ t('APP.LOGOUT') }}</button>
      </template>
    </div>

  • lines 21–24: logout, followed by the login page. [.catch(() => {})]: even if the server does not respond, the client disconnects;
  • line 31: the menus only appear once logged in, depending on the role: “My area” for a patient, “Doctors” and “Patients” for the ADMIN. This is simply for display convenience; true security is provided by the server;
  • line 34: the menu on the displayed page is assigned the class [active];
  • lines 53–63: the FR / EN buttons. [:aria-pressed] indicates to screen readers which button is pressed;
