docs.title: 6.1.2. The configuration
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 16-i18n/src/i18n.ts - the configuration of vue-i18n
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// vue-i18n is the translation library of Vue.js. We provide it with:
//   - a DICTIONARY per language (files locales/fr.json, locales/en.json),
//     where each text has a KEY ("HOME.HELLO");
//   - the starting language (here: the one stored in localStorage, otherwise
//     the browser's one, otherwise English);
//   - date and number formats specific to each language.
// In the components, t('HOME.HELLO', { name: 'Marie' }) returns the
// text of the CURRENT language; changing the language updates the whole page.
//
// It is, on the client side, the same principle as the NestJS course (dictionaries
// i18n/*.json + helper {{t}}) - but the translation is now done in
// the browser, and changing the language no longer asks anything of the server.
// =========================================================================

import { createI18n } from 'vue-i18n';
import fr from './locales/fr.json';
import en from './locales/en.json';

export type Language = 'fr' | 'en';
export const LANGUAGE_KEY = 'example16.language';

function initialLanguage(): Language {
  const stored = localStorage.getItem(LANGUAGE_KEY);
  if (stored === 'fr' || stored === 'en') {
    return stored;
  }
  return navigator.language.startsWith('fr') ? 'fr' : 'en';
}

// the type of the messages: that of the English dictionary (the "model")
type Messages = typeof en;

export const i18n = createI18n<[Messages], Language>({
  legacy: false, // the "Composition" API (useI18n), that of <script setup>
  locale: initialLanguage(),
  fallbackLocale: 'en', // a key missing in French: the English one is used
  messages: { fr, en },
  // d(date, 'long') and n(number, 'euros'): formats specific to each language
  datetimeFormats: {
    fr: { long: { dateStyle: 'full' } },
    en: { long: { dateStyle: 'full' } },
  },
  numberFormats: {
    fr: { euros: { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' } },
    en: { euros: { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' } },
  },
});
  • line 19: [Vite] can import a JSON file: this returns an object;
  • lines 25–31: the language stored in [localStorage], otherwise the browser’s language ([navigator.language]), otherwise English;
  • lines 36–50: the configuration object:
    • [legacy: false]: the Composition API ([useI18n]), that of [<script setup>];
    • [fallbackLocale: 'en']: a key missing from the French dictionary is taken from the English dictionary;
    • [datetimeFormats], [numberFormats]: date and number formats specific to each language.
import { createApp } from 'vue';
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css';
import App from './App.vue';
import { i18n } from './i18n';

// app.use(i18n): t(), d(), n() become available in all the components
createApp(App).use(i18n).mount('#app');

docs.title: 6.1.3. The page
docs.text:
<!--
  =========================================================================
  16-i18n/src/App.vue - a translated page
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - t('KEY')                  a text;
    - t('KEY', { name: ... })   a text with parameters ({name} in the dictionary);
    - t('KEY', n)               a plural: "none | one | {n}" depending on n;
    - d(date, 'long')           a date, in the format of the language;
    - n(number, 'euros')        a number, in the format of the language;
    - locale                    the current language: modifying it translates everything again.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref, watch } from 'vue';
import { useI18n } from 'vue-i18n';
import { LANGUAGE_KEY, type Language } from './i18n';

const { t, d, n, locale } = useI18n();
const count = ref(2);

// on each change of language: it is stored, and the lang attribute of the
// page is updated (useful for screen readers, spell checkers)
watch(
  locale,
  (language) => {
    localStorage.setItem(LANGUAGE_KEY, language);
    document.documentElement.lang = language;
    document.title = t('APP.TITLE');
  },
  { immediate: true },
);

function choose(language: Language): void {
  locale.value = language;
}

// what the RdvMedecins server would return (see the chapter on the black box)
const serverResponses = [
  { statusCode: 409, key: 'ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN' },
  { statusCode: 429, key: 'ERRORS.TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS', params: { minutes: '15' } },
];
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 720px">
    <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-3">
      <h1 class="h3 mb-0">{{ t('APP.TITLE') }}</h1>
      <div class="btn-group btn-group-sm" role="group" :aria-label="t('APP.LANGUAGE')">
        <button class="btn" :class="locale === 'fr' ? 'btn-primary' : 'btn-outline-primary'" @click="choose('fr')">FR</button>
        <button class="btn" :class="locale === 'en' ? 'btn-primary' : 'btn-outline-primary'" @click="choose('en')">EN</button>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="card p-3 mb-3">
      <p>{{ t('HOME.HELLO', { name: 'Marie' }) }}</p>
      <p>{{ t('HOME.TODAY', { date: d(new Date(), 'long') }) }}</p>
      <p>{{ t('HOME.PRICE', { price: n(1234.5, 'euros') }) }}</p>
      <!-- t(key, number) chooses the right plural form -->
      <p class="fw-bold">{{ t('HOME.APPOINTMENTS', count) }}</p>
      <div class="d-flex gap-2">
        <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-success" @click="count++">{{ t('HOME.ADD') }}</button>
        <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" :disabled="count === 0" @click="count--">{{ t('HOME.REMOVE') }}</button>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="card p-3">
      <h2 class="h6">{{ t('SERVER.TITLE') }}</h2>
      <p>{{ t('SERVER.EXPLANATION') }}</p>
      <ul class="mb-0">
        <li v-for="r in serverResponses" :key="r.key">
          <code>{{ JSON.stringify(r) }}</code><br>
          <!-- the server's key IS a key of the dictionary; params provides its parameters -->
          → {{ t(r.key, r.params ?? {}) }}
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
  • line 18: translation tools:
    • [t(key, params)]: a text;
    • [t(key, n)]: a plural;
    • [d(date, 'long')]: a date, in the language's format;
    • [n(number, 'euros')]: a number, in the language's format;
    • [locale]: the current language, a [ref]. Changing it re-translates the entire page;
  • lines 23–30: Each time the language is changed, the selection is saved and the page’s [lang] attribute is updated (useful for screen readers and spell-checkers);
  • lines 38–41: two error responses, as returned by the server [RdvMedecins];
  • line 73: the key sent by the server is a dictionary key; its parameters are those of the message.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is HERE.

The document’s codes are HERE.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s AI Claude. It follows the course “Step-by-Step Introduction to the NestJS Web Framework,” from which it shifts the perspective:

  • In the course [NestJS], the server generates the pages HTML (view engine [Handlebars]); the browser simply displays them;
  • in this course, the pages are generated in the browser by an application [Vue.js]; the server, now reduced to a simple server JSON, provides only data.

The application’s pages, however, remain unchanged: they are those of the [RdvMedecins] application already presented with the other frameworks (login with CAPTCHA, doctor’s schedule, appointment window, patient portal, doctor and client management, account creation, French and English).

The document follows the same structure as its predecessors: first, numerous short examples, each focusing on a specific concept of [Vue.js], followed by a complete case study—the [Vue.js] client for the [RdvMedecins] application—with all files fully commented.

There are already two courses available on [Vue.js]: “Introduction to the VUE.JS Framework Through Examples” (2019), written for [Vue.js] 2, and “An Example of a Vue.js Client/Server / NestJS (2026), which covers both the server and the client. This document differs from those in its approach: the server is treated as a black box, with only the API and JSON of interest to us, and we learn [Vue.js] step by step before tackling the complete client.

docs.title: 1.1. The Role of Vue.js in a Web Application
docs.text:
The application has two parts, which communicate with each other only through HTTP requests:

  • 1: The [Vue.js] application, running in the browser, sends a HTTP request to the server, for example, [GET /api/schedule?doctorId=1&day=2026-10-05];
  • 2: The server responds with data JSON: this doctor’s schedule for that day. It does not generate any pages;
  • 3: Using this data, [Vue.js] updates the page displayed in the browser without reloading it.

The following diagram compares the two architectures:

The browser loads only a single, nearly empty page—HTML—at startup. Everything else is generated by [JavaScript] code: this is known as a single-page application (SPA, for [Single Page Application]). When the user clicks on an internal link, no page is requested from the server: the [Vue.js] router changes the displayed URL and replaces the page’s content.

[Vue.js] is a [JavaScript] framework created in 2014 by Evan You. It is based on two ideas:

  • components: the interface is broken down into reusable pieces (a navigation bar, a form field, a confirmation window, etc.), each written in a [.vue] file that combines its HTML, code, and style;
  • reactivity: a component’s data is “observed.” When any of it changes, [Vue.js] automatically updates the parts of the page that display it. We never write code that directly modifies the page.

We will use [Vue.js] 3, written in [TypeScript], with its most recent version: the Composition API and the [<script setup>] tag.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • [Node.js] 22 (or at least 20.19) and its package manager [npm];
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor, with the [Vue (Official)] extension;
  • a recent browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]), if possible with the extension [Vue.js devtools];
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays the raw HTTP responses;
  • the DBMS [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, the one for [Laragon] under [Windows]: it is required for the JSON server, as described in the chapter introducing it.

The libraries are those for the [package.json] files: [Vue.js] 3.5, [Vite] 7 (the development and build tool), [vue-router] 4 (the router), [Pinia] 3 (shared state), [vue-i18n] 11 (languages), [TypeScript] 5.9, [Bootstrap] 5.3.

docs.title: 1.3. Examples
docs.text:
The codes in the document are organized into three folders:

deliverable/
├── examples-vuejs/          the 20 small Vue.js examples
├── rdvmedecins-nestjs-json/ the RdvMedecins JSON server (the "black box")
└── rdvmedecins-vuejs/       the Vue.js client of the case study

The examples folder contains one subfolder per example:

examples-vuejs/
├── 01-first-application/
├── 02-reactivity/
├── ...
├── 20-server-errors/
├── common/              code shared by examples 19 and 20
├── node_modules/
├── index.html           the table of contents of the examples
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── vite.config.ts

All examples share the same libraries, which are declared in [examples-vuejs/package.json]. They are installed once, in a console opened to the [examples-vuejs] folder (in [VS Code]: Terminal menu / New Terminal):

npm install

Then launch the [Vite] development server:

npm run dev

A single server, on port 5173, serves all twenty examples. The address http://localhost:5173/ displays their summary:

You can navigate from one example to another by following the links (http://localhost:5173/01-first-application/, http://localhost:5173/02-reactivity/...). The [Vite] server does not need to be restarted: every file that is modified and saved is immediately recompiled, and the browser page updates automatically. You can stop it by entering [Ctrl-C] in the console.

Examples 17 through 20 query the JSON and [RdvMedecins] servers: you will need to have them installed and running, as explained in the chapter dedicated to them.

docs.title: 4. Routing
docs.text: A [Vue.js] application loads only one page, HTML. However, the [RdvMedecins] application has a login page, a calendar page, a “My area” page... Each has its own URL ([/login], [/schedule], [/my-area]), which can be bookmarked, and the browser’s Back and Forward buttons work. This is the work of the router, the [vue-router] library.

docs.title: 4.1. Example 13: The Router
docs.text:
The router is added to the application in [main.ts]:

// =========================================================================
// 13-router/src/main.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// app.use(router): the router is added to the application. The components
// <RouterLink> and <RouterView> then become usable everywhere.
// =========================================================================

import { createApp } from 'vue';
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css';
import App from './App.vue';
import { router } from './router';

createApp(App).use(router).mount('#app');
  • Line 13: [app.use(...)] installs an extension ([plugin]): The components [<RouterLink>] and [<RouterView>], and the functions [useRoute()] and [useRouter()], become available everywhere.

The example data, "hard-coded":

// "hard-coded" data, so as not to depend on a server in this example
export interface Doctor {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  firstName: string;
  lastName: string;
  specialty: string;
}

export const DOCTORS: Doctor[] = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Mme', firstName: 'Marie', lastName: 'PELISSIER', specialty: 'general practitioner' },
  { id: 2, title: 'Mr', firstName: 'Paul', lastName: 'TATOU', specialty: 'pediatrician' },
  { id: 3, title: 'Melle', firstName: 'Sophie', lastName: 'DUPONT', specialty: 'general practitioner' },
];

The routes:

// =========================================================================
// 13-router/src/router.ts - the ROUTES of the application
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A Vue.js application is a single-page application (SPA: Single
// Page Application): the browser loads only ONE HTML page. When an
// internal link is clicked, no request is sent to the server:
// the router changes the address displayed by the browser, and replaces the
// component displayed in <RouterView>.
//
// A route associates a PATH with a COMPONENT (called a "view", in the
// sense of a screen of the application):
//   '/doctors/:id'        :id is a parameter (/doctors/2 -> id = "2");
//   '/:pathMatch(.*)*'    any path: the "not found" page
//                         (the most precise route always wins).
//
// createWebHashHistory: the addresses look like /13-router/#/doctors/2.
// Everything after the # stays in the browser: reloading the page (F5)
// always requests /13-router/ again, which exists. It is the simplest mode
// when the server knows nothing about the router - here, the Vite server, which
// serves twenty examples at once. The case study will use "clean"
// addresses (createWebHistory: /schedule, /doctors...).
// =========================================================================

import { createRouter, createWebHashHistory } from 'vue-router';
import Home from './views/Home.vue';
import DoctorList from './views/DoctorList.vue';
import DoctorDetail from './views/DoctorDetail.vue';
import Search from './views/Search.vue';
import NotFoundPage from './views/NotFoundPage.vue';

export const router = createRouter({
  history: createWebHashHistory(),
  routes: [
    { path: '/', name: 'home', component: Home },
    { path: '/doctors', name: 'doctors', component: DoctorList },
    // props: true -> the :id parameter is passed to the component as a PROP
    // (the component then no longer depends on the router: easier to reuse)
    { path: '/doctors/:id', name: 'doctor', component: DoctorDetail, props: true },
    { path: '/search', name: 'search', component: Search },
    // a redirection: the old address leads to the new one
    { path: '/physicians', redirect: '/doctors' },
    { path: '/:pathMatch(.*)*', name: 'not-found', component: NotFoundPage },
  ],
});
  • Lines 33–43: A route associates a path with a component, which is called a “view” (in the sense of an application screen; this has nothing to do with the [Handlebars] views from the [NestJS] course, except for their role);
  • line 34: a route can have a name, which is more stable than its path for creating links;
  • Line 38: [:id] is a parameter: [/doctors/2] displays [DoctorDetail] along with [id = "2"]. The option [props: true] passes it to the component as a prop: the component is then no longer dependent on the router;
  • line 41: a redirect: the address [/physicians] leads to [/doctors];
  • line 42: an arbitrary path: the “page not found” page. It only receives addresses that no other route recognizes: [vue-router] sorts routes by the precision of their path; the most precise one takes precedence (it is still placed last for readability);
  • line 32: history mode. With [createWebHashHistory], the addresses take the form [/13-router/#/doctors/2]: anything following [#] is never sent to the server, and reloading the page (F5) always requests [/13-router/], which exists. This is the simplest approach when the server does not know the client’s routes, which is the case for the server at [Vite], which serves twenty examples at a time. The case study will use [createWebHistory] and “clean” addresses ([/schedule]), which requires a little extra effort on the server’s part.

The application’s “shell”:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  13-router/src/App.vue - the "shell" of the application
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - <RouterLink to="...">: an internal link. It produces an <a> tag,
      but a click does not reload the page: it is the router that acts.
      The link of the displayed page receives the class "router-link-active"
      (here replaced by "active", the Bootstrap one);
    - <RouterView />: the place where the component of the current route
      is displayed.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { RouterLink, RouterView, useRoute } from 'vue-router';

// useRoute(): the current route (path, parameters, query...), reactive
const route = useRoute();
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Example 13 - the router</h1>
    <nav class="nav nav-pills mb-3">
      <RouterLink class="nav-link" active-class="active" to="/">Home</RouterLink>
      <!-- to can be an object: the NAME of the route rather than its path -->
      <RouterLink class="nav-link" active-class="active" :to="{ name: 'doctors' }">Doctors</RouterLink>
      <RouterLink class="nav-link" active-class="active" :to="{ name: 'search', query: { q: 'general practitioner' } }">Search</RouterLink>
      <RouterLink class="nav-link" to="/physicians">/physicians (redirection)</RouterLink>
      <RouterLink class="nav-link" to="/unknown-page">Broken link</RouterLink>
    </nav>
    <p class="small text-muted">current route: <code>{{ route.fullPath }}</code> (name: {{ String(route.name) }})</p>
    <div class="card p-3">
      <RouterView />
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
  • line 17: the current route (path, parameters, [query]...), which is dynamic: the template updates when it changes;
  • line 24: [<RouterLink>] generates a [<a>] tag, but clicking does not reload the page: the router changes the address and the displayed component. The link on the current page is assigned the class specified by [active-class] (here, [active], which is the class of [Bootstrap]);
  • line 26: the destination can be an object: the route name rather than its path;
  • line 27: a link with query parameters: [/search?q=general practitioner];
  • line 33: the location where the current route component is displayed.

The pages. The list of doctors generates links with parameters:

<!-- 13-router/src/views/DoctorList.vue - links with a parameter -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { RouterLink } from 'vue-router';
import { DOCTORS } from '../data';
</script>

<template>
  <ul class="mb-0">
    <li v-for="m in DOCTORS" :key="m.id">
      <!-- { name, params }: the router builds the address /doctors/2 itself -->
      <RouterLink :to="{ name: 'doctor', params: { id: m.id } }">{{ m.title }} {{ m.firstName }} {{ m.lastName }}</RouterLink>
    </li>
  </ul>
</template>
  • line 11: the router itself constructs the address [/doctors/2] from the route name and its parameters.

A doctor’s page:

<!--
  13-router/src/views/DoctorDetail.vue - a page with a parameter
  The id arrives as a PROP (props: true in router.ts), as a string.
  useRouter() gives the router itself, to navigate BY CODE.
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import { useRouter } from 'vue-router';
import { DOCTORS } from '../data';

const props = defineProps<{ id: string }>();
const router = useRouter();

// computed: when going from /doctors/1 to /doctors/2, Vue REUSES the
// same component and only changes the prop - the computed follows
const doctor = computed(() => DOCTORS.find((m) => m.id === Number(props.id)) ?? null);
const next = computed(() => (Number(props.id) % DOCTORS.length) + 1);
</script>

<template>
  <div v-if="doctor">
    <h2 class="h5">{{ doctor.title }} {{ doctor.firstName }} {{ doctor.lastName }}</h2>
    <p>Specialty: {{ doctor.specialty }}</p>
    <div class="d-flex gap-2">
      <!-- navigation by code: router.push(...) or router.back() -->
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" @click="router.back()">Back</button>
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" @click="router.push({ name: 'doctor', params: { id: next } })">Next doctor</button>
    </div>
  </div>
  <p v-else class="text-danger mb-0">Doctor no. {{ id }} does not exist.</p>
</template>
  • Line 11: The parameter [:id] is passed as a prop, in string form;
  • line 12: the router itself, to navigate through the code;
  • line 16: switching from [/doctors/1] to [/doctors/2] does not recreate the component: [Vue.js] reuses the one that is displayed and only changes its prop. A [computed] follows this change; code placed in [onMounted] would, however, be executed only once;
  • lines 26 and 27: return to the previous page, go to another page.

The search is a page entirely described by its URL, just like the GET form from the [NestJS] course:

<!--
  13-router/src/views/Search.vue - a page driven by the QUERY of the URL
  (/search?q=pediatrician). As with the GET form of the NestJS course, the
  page is entirely described by its address: it can be
  bookmarked, reloaded, navigated back to.
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed, ref, watch } from 'vue';
import { useRoute, useRouter } from 'vue-router';
import { DOCTORS } from '../data';

const route = useRoute();
const router = useRouter();

// the input field starts with the value of the URL...
const input = ref(String(route.query.q ?? ''));
// ... and follows the URL if it changes (Back button for example)
watch(() => route.query.q, (q) => (input.value = String(q ?? '')));

const results = computed(() => {
  const q = String(route.query.q ?? '').toLowerCase();
  return DOCTORS.filter((m) => `${m.firstName} ${m.lastName} ${m.specialty}`.toLowerCase().includes(q));
});

function search(): void {
  // we change the URL; the display follows the URL (computed above)
  router.push({ name: 'search', query: { q: input.value } });
}
</script>

<template>
  <form class="d-flex gap-2 mb-3" @submit.prevent="search">
    <input v-model="input" class="form-control" placeholder="name or specialty">
    <button class="btn btn-primary">Search</button>
  </form>
  <ul class="mb-0">
    <li v-for="m in results" :key="m.id">{{ m.firstName }} {{ m.lastName }} ({{ m.specialty }})</li>
  </ul>
</template>
  • line 16: [route.query] contains the parameters of URL ([?q=...]);
  • line 18: if URL changes (Previous button), the field follows;
  • line 20: the results depend on URL, not on the field;
  • line 27: searching changes the URL; the display updates accordingly. You can bookmark the search, reload it, or go back.

docs.title: 4.2. Example 14: Navigation Restrictions
docs.text:
Some pages require you to be logged in, while others require a specific role. This example simulates a login without a server:

// =========================================================================
// 14-guards/src/session.ts - a SIMULATED session (without a server)
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The logged-in user, in a ref declared at MODULE level: all
// the files that import this module share the same one. (Example 15 will do
// the same thing, better, with Pinia; example 18 with a real server.)
// =========================================================================

import { ref } from 'vue';

export type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'DOCTOR' | 'USER';

export interface User {
  login: string;
  role: Role;
}

export const user = ref<User | null>(null);

// three "hard-coded" accounts (password = login)
const ACCOUNTS: Record<string, Role> = { admin: 'ADMIN', pelissier: 'DOCTOR', martin: 'USER' };

export function logIn(login: string, password: string): boolean {
  const role = ACCOUNTS[login];
  if (role === undefined || password !== login) {
    return false;
  }
  user.value = { login, role };
  return true;
}

export function logOut(): void {
  user.value = null;
}
  • Line 18: a [ref] declared at the module level: all files that import [session.ts] share the same one.

The routes and their guards:

// =========================================================================
// 14-guards/src/router.ts - PROTECTED routes
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// meta: free information attached to a route. Here:
//   - meta.requiresLogin: the page requires being logged in;
//   - meta.roles        : the authorized roles (absent = all).
//
// router.beforeEach(...): a NAVIGATION GUARD, executed before EACH
// page change. It returns:
//   - true                : the navigation continues;
//   - another address     : redirection;
// It is the client-side equivalent of the NestJS guards (JwtAuthGuard,
// RolesGuard) - with a FUNDAMENTAL difference: a client guard is
// only a comfort. The client code is in the hands of the user, who
// can modify it at will. The real protection of the data remains that
// of the SERVER (see the chapter on the black box).
// =========================================================================

import { createRouter, createWebHashHistory } from 'vue-router';
import { user, type Role } from './session';
import Home from './views/Home.vue';
import Login from './views/Login.vue';
import Schedule from './views/Schedule.vue';

// we declare to TypeScript the meta properties we use
declare module 'vue-router' {
  interface RouteMeta {
    requiresLogin?: boolean;
    roles?: Role[];
  }
}

export const router = createRouter({
  history: createWebHashHistory(),
  routes: [
    { path: '/', component: Home },
    { path: '/login', component: Login },
    { path: '/schedule', component: Schedule, meta: { requiresLogin: true } },
    {
      path: '/administration',
      // LAZY loading: the code of this component is only downloaded
      // on the first visit of the page (Vite makes a separate file of it)
      component: () => import('./views/Administration.vue'),
      meta: { requiresLogin: true, roles: ['ADMIN'] },
    },
  ],
});

router.beforeEach((to) => {
  if (to.meta.requiresLogin && user.value === null) {
    // not logged in: to the login page, remembering where we wanted to go
    return { path: '/login', query: { redirect: to.fullPath } };
  }
  if (to.meta.roles && user.value && !to.meta.roles.includes(user.value.role)) {
    // logged in, but not with the right role: back to the home page, with a reason
    return { path: '/', query: { denied: to.fullPath } };
  }
  return true;
});
  • Lines 26–31: We declare in [TypeScript] the properties that we will store in the [meta] field of the routes. [meta] accepts arbitrary data; declaring these properties allows them to be used without type casting;
  • line 38: the page requires the user to be logged in;
  • line 43: deferred loading: the code for this component is downloaded only on the first visit to the page. [Vite] stores it in a separate file. This way, an application loads only what it needs at startup;
  • Lines 49–59: a navigation guard, executed before EACH page change. It returns [true] to allow access, or another address to redirect to:
    • not logged in: redirects to [/login], retaining the requested page in the [redirect] parameter;
    • logged in without the correct role: returns to the home page, with the reason for denial.

The login page redirects the user to where they wanted to go:

<!--
  14-guards/src/views/Login.vue
  After logging in, the user is sent back to the page they wanted to
  open (parameter ?redirect=... set by the guard), or to the home page.
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue';
import { useRoute, useRouter } from 'vue-router';
import { logIn } from '../session';

const route = useRoute();
const router = useRouter();
const login = ref('');
const password = ref('');
const error = ref(false);

function submit(): void {
  error.value = !logIn(login.value.trim(), password.value);
  if (!error.value) {
    const redirect = route.query.redirect;
    // only an INTERNAL path is accepted: it starts with /, but not with //
    // (//site.com/... designates ANOTHER site) - no redirection to another site
    const internal = typeof redirect === 'string' && redirect.startsWith('/') && !redirect.startsWith('//');
    router.push(internal ? redirect : '/');
  }
}
</script>

<template>
  <p v-if="route.query.redirect" class="alert alert-warning">Log in to open {{ route.query.redirect }}.</p>
  <form class="d-flex flex-wrap gap-2" @submit.prevent="submit">
    <input v-model="login" class="form-control w-auto" placeholder="login" autocomplete="username">
    <input v-model="password" type="password" class="form-control w-auto" placeholder="password" autocomplete="current-password">
    <button class="btn btn-primary">Log in</button>
  </form>
  <p v-if="error" class="text-danger mt-2 mb-0">Incorrect login or password.</p>
</template>
  • Line 23: Only an INTERNAL path is accepted: it starts with [/], but not with [//] ([//site.com/...] refers to ANOTHER site). Redirecting to a full URL received in the URL would allow a malicious link to send the user, immediately after logging in, to another site imitating ours (a vulnerability known as [open redirect]).

The other files are very short:

<script setup lang="ts">
import { RouterLink, RouterView, useRouter } from 'vue-router';
import { logOut, user } from './session';

const router = useRouter();

function onLogOut(): void {
  logOut();
  router.push('/');
}
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 720px">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Example 14 - navigation guards</h1>
    <nav class="d-flex gap-3 align-items-center mb-3">
      <RouterLink to="/">Home</RouterLink>
      <RouterLink to="/schedule">Schedule (logged in)</RouterLink>
      <RouterLink to="/administration">Administration (ADMIN)</RouterLink>
      <span class="ms-auto">
        <template v-if="user">
          {{ user.login }} <span class="badge text-bg-primary">{{ user.role }}</span>
          <button class="btn btn-sm btn-link" @click="onLogOut">log out</button>
        </template>
        <RouterLink v-else to="/login">log in</RouterLink>
      </span>
    </nav>
    <div class="card p-3"><RouterView /></div>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup lang="ts">
import { useRoute } from 'vue-router';
const route = useRoute();
</script>

<template>
  <!-- ?denied=...: set by the guard when the role does not fit -->
  <p v-if="route.query.denied" class="alert alert-danger">Your role does not allow you to open {{ route.query.denied }}.</p>
  <p class="mb-0">Public page. Try the two other links, logged in or not (admin, pelissier, martin - password = login).</p>
</template>

Clicking on “Administration (ADMIN)” while not logged in takes you to the login page:

When logged in with the account [martin] (role [USER]), the guard denies access to the administration page:

A FUNDAMENTAL note: a navigation guard is merely a convenience (to avoid displaying an unnecessary page). The client-side code is in the user’s hands; they can read and modify it in their browser. True data protection comes from the server, which verifies the user’s identity and role with every request. We’ll see this with the [RdvMedecins] server.

docs.title: 5.1. Example 15: Shared State with Pinia
docs.text:
In an application, certain data is relevant to many components: the logged-in user, the shopping cart, etc. Example 11 shared this data with [provide] / [inject], while Example 14 used a [ref] module. [Pinia], the official library for [Vue.js] for shared state, organizes this into stores and makes them visible in the [Vue.js devtools] extension.

It is installed in [main.ts]:

// =========================================================================
// 15-pinia/src/main.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// app.use(createPinia()): Pinia is installed, the official Vue.js library
// for SHARED state management. The "stores" defined
// next are accessible from any component.
// =========================================================================

import { createApp } from 'vue';
import { createPinia } from 'pinia';
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css';
import App from './App.vue';

createApp(App).use(createPinia()).mount('#app');

The first store, the shopping cart:

// =========================================================================
// 15-pinia/src/stores/cart.ts - a Pinia STORE
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// defineStore('cart', () => { ... }): a store written like a composable
// ("setup" style):
//   - the refs are the STATE of the store;
//   - the computed values, its GETTERS (computed values);
//   - the functions, its ACTIONS (what modifies the state).
// Difference with a composable (example 11): the store only exists in ONE
// copy for the whole application. All the components that call
// useCartStore() receive the SAME cart. It lives as long as the application
// lives: it survives the removal of a component... but not the reloading of
// the page (F5), which restarts the application.
// =========================================================================

import { computed, ref } from 'vue';
import { defineStore } from 'pinia';

export interface Item {
  label: string;
  price: number;
}

export const useCartStore = defineStore('cart', () => {
  const items = ref<Item[]>([]);

  const count = computed(() => items.value.length);
  const total = computed(() => items.value.reduce((s, a) => s + a.price, 0));

  function add(item: Item): void {
    items.value.push(item);
  }
  function clear(): void {
    items.value = [];
  }

  // everything that is returned is part of the store
  return { items, count, total, add, clear };
});
  • lines 24–39: [defineStore(name, function)] defines a store in the “setup” style, like a composable: the [ref] are its state, the [computed] are its getters, and the functions are its actions; it exposes what the function returns;
  • The difference from a composable: there is only one instance of the store for the entire application. All components that call [useCartStore()] receive the SAME shopping cart. It lives as long as the application lives: it survives the removal of a component... but not a page reload (F5), which restarts the application.

A second store, however, survives the page reload:

// =========================================================================
// 15-pinia/src/stores/preferences.ts - a store that survives F5
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// For a piece of data to survive the reloading of the page, or the closing
// of the browser, it must be stored IN the browser: localStorage (a
// small key -> string dictionary, specific to each site).
//   - at startup, the store reads localStorage again;
//   - watch(..., { deep: true }) rewrites localStorage on each change.
// NEVER store sensitive data there (password, token): any script
// of the page can read localStorage.
// =========================================================================

import { ref, watch } from 'vue';
import { defineStore } from 'pinia';

const KEY = 'example15.preferences';

interface Preferences {
  dark: boolean;
  size: number; // text size, in px
}

function read(): Preferences {
  try {
    return { dark: false, size: 16, ...JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY) ?? '{}') };
  } catch {
    return { dark: false, size: 16 }; // unreadable content: default values
  }
}

export const usePreferencesStore = defineStore('preferences', () => {
  const preferences = ref<Preferences>(read());

  watch(preferences, (p) => localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(p)), { deep: true });

  return { preferences };
});
  • Lines 23–29: Upon startup, the browser re-reads [localStorage], a small key/value dictionary that the browser stores for each site, even after the browser is closed. If the content is unreadable, the default values are used;
  • Line 34: [{ deep: true }]: [watch] also reacts to changes in the object’s properties. Each change is rewritten to [localStorage].

NEVER store sensitive data (passwords, tokens) in [localStorage]: any script executed on the page can read [localStorage].

The components:

<!-- 15-pinia/src/components/Shop.vue - ADDS to the shared cart -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useCartStore, type Item } from '../stores/cart';

const cart = useCartStore();
const products: Item[] = [
  { label: 'Consultation', price: 30 },
  { label: 'Vaccine', price: 12.5 },
];
</script>

<template>
  <div class="card p-3 h-100">
    <h2 class="h6">Shop</h2>
    <button v-for="p in products" :key="p.label" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary mb-2" @click="cart.add(p)">
      + {{ p.label }} (€{{ p.price }})
    </button>
  </div>
</template>
  • Line 5: The store is used as a reactive object: [cart.add(p)];
<!--
  15-pinia/src/components/CartSummary.vue - READS the same cart
  storeToRefs: to DESTRUCTURE a store without losing reactivity
  (const { count } = cart would give a simple, frozen copy).
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { storeToRefs } from 'pinia';
import { useCartStore } from '../stores/cart';

const cart = useCartStore();
const { count, total } = storeToRefs(cart);
</script>

<template>
  <div class="card p-3 h-100">
    <h2 class="h6">Cart</h2>
    <p class="mb-2">{{ count }} item(s), €{{ total }}</p>
    <!-- the actions, for their part, can be destructured or called directly -->
    <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger align-self-start" :disabled="count === 0" @click="cart.clear()">Clear</button>
  </div>
</template>
  • line 11: to destructure a store without losing reactivity. [const { count } = cart] would return a simple copy, frozen at the current value; [storeToRefs] returns [ref] instances linked to the store. Actions, on the other hand, can be destructured or called directly.
<!-- 15-pinia/src/components/LocalCounter.vue - a LOCAL state, which disappears with the component -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue';
const clicks = ref(0);
</script>

<template>
  <div class="card p-3 h-100">
    <h2 class="h6">Local state</h2>
    <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary align-self-start" @click="clicks++">{{ clicks }} click(s)</button>
  </div>
</template>

<!--
  =========================================================================
  15-pinia/src/App.vue - three "scopes" of data on the client side
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Same question as example 23 of the NestJS course (application,
  request, client scope), transposed to the browser:
    - the LOCAL state of a component (LocalCounter) disappears with it;
    - the state of a STORE (the cart) is shared by all the components and
      survives their removal - but not F5;
    - the state stored in localStorage (the preferences) survives F5 and the
      closing of the browser.
  Uncheck then check the box again, then reload the page: compare.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue';
import { usePreferencesStore } from './stores/preferences';
import Shop from './components/Shop.vue';
import CartSummary from './components/CartSummary.vue';
import LocalCounter from './components/LocalCounter.vue';

const prefs = usePreferencesStore();
const areaVisible = ref(true);
</script>

<template>
  <div :class="{ 'bg-dark text-light': prefs.preferences.dark }" :style="{ fontSize: prefs.preferences.size + 'px' }" class="min-vh-100">
    <div class="container py-4">
      <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Example 15 - a shared state with Pinia</h1>
      <div class="d-flex flex-wrap gap-4 mb-3">
        <label class="form-check-label"><input v-model="prefs.preferences.dark" type="checkbox" class="form-check-input"> dark theme</label>
        <label>text size <input v-model.number="prefs.preferences.size" type="range" min="12" max="22"> {{ prefs.preferences.size }} px</label>
        <label class="form-check-label"><input v-model="areaVisible" type="checkbox" class="form-check-input"> show the area</label>
      </div>
      <div v-if="areaVisible" class="row g-3 text-body">
        <div class="col-md-4"><Shop /></div>
        <div class="col-md-4"><CartSummary /></div>
        <div class="col-md-4"><LocalCounter /></div>
      </div>
      <p class="mt-3 mb-2">Outside the area, a second summary of the SAME cart (it stays there when the area disappears):</p>
      <div class="text-body"><CartSummary /></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
  • Line 35: Unchecking “show the area” removes the three components from the page;
  • line 41: a second summary of the same shopping cart, outside the area.

Same question as Example 23 from course [NestJS] (application, query, and client scopes), adapted for the browser:

DataWhere?LifetimeThe counter for LocalCounterthe component's local statedisappears along with the componentthe shopping carta Pinia storethe entire application, up to F5preferencesa Pinia store + localStoragesurvives F5 and browser closure

Two items added and two clicks:

The section was removed and the dark theme was selected: the shopping cart is still there; if the section is displayed again, the local counter resets to zero:

docs.title: 3. The Components
docs.text: So far, each example has fit into a single component, [App.vue]. A real application contains dozens of them: a navigation bar, forms, windows... Each component is a self-contained piece of the interface (its HTML, its code, its style) and is reusable. This chapter shows how components fit together and communicate.

docs.title: 3.1. Example 07: Components and Their Props
docs.text:
The example displays one card per doctor. The card is a component, [DoctorCard.vue], used three times by its parent, [App.vue].

The doctor type, shared by both components, is in a regular [TypeScript] file:

// the data type shared by the parent (App.vue) and the child (DoctorCard.vue)
export interface Doctor {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  firstName: string;
  lastName: string;
  specialty: string;
  available: boolean;
}

The child component:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  07-components/src/components/DoctorCard.vue - a CHILD component
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  It receives its data from its parent through PROPS (properties), declared
  with defineProps. The TypeScript type of the props is checked at
  compile time: <DoctorCard :doctor="42"> would be rejected.

  Golden rule: a component NEVER MODIFIES its props. The data
  flows down from the parent to the child ("one-way data flow"); to
  request a change, the child emits an event (see example 08).
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import type { Doctor } from '../doctor';

// withDefaults: a default value for the optional props (?)
const props = withDefaults(
  defineProps<{
    doctor: Doctor;
    rank: number;
    compact?: boolean;
  }>(),
  { compact: false },
);

// a computed based on a prop: recomputed if the parent changes the prop
const initials = computed(() => `${props.doctor.firstName[0]}${props.doctor.lastName[0]}`);
</script>

<template>
  <div class="card h-100" :class="{ 'border-success': doctor.available }">
    <div class="card-body d-flex gap-3 align-items-center">
      <div class="initials">{{ initials }}</div>
      <div>
        <!-- in the template, the props are used directly by their name -->
        <h2 class="h6 mb-1">{{ rank }}. {{ doctor.title }} {{ doctor.firstName }} {{ doctor.lastName }}</h2>
        <p v-if="!compact" class="mb-0 text-muted small">{{ doctor.specialty }}</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>

<style scoped>
.initials {
  width: 2.5rem;
  height: 2.5rem;
  border-radius: 50%;
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  background: #0d6efd;
  color: white;
  font-weight: bold;
}
</style>
  • Line 16: [import type] imports only one type: nothing from this import remains in the resulting [JavaScript];
  • Lines 19–26: [defineProps<{...}>()] declares the component’s props—that is, the data it receives from its parent—along with their types. A prop followed by [?] is optional; [withDefaults] gives it a default value. [defineProps] does not need to be imported: it is a “macro” recognized by the [.vue] file compiler;
  • Line 29: In the script, the props are read via the [props] object. [computed] tracks the props: if the parent changes the assigned doctor, the initials are recalculated;
  • line 38: In the template, props are used directly by name;
  • line 39: a prop can modify the display.

The parent:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  07-components/src/App.vue - the PARENT component
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  It imports the DoctorCard component and uses it as a new
  HTML tag, <DoctorCard>, as many times as needed: a component
  is a REUSABLE piece of interface, with its own data, its
  template and its style.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue';
// in <script setup>, an imported component is immediately usable in the template
import DoctorCard from './components/DoctorCard.vue';
import type { Doctor } from './doctor';

const doctors = ref<Doctor[]>([
  { id: 1, title: 'Mme', firstName: 'Marie', lastName: 'PELISSIER', specialty: 'general practitioner', available: true },
  { id: 2, title: 'Mr', firstName: 'Paul', lastName: 'TATOU', specialty: 'pediatrician', available: false },
  { id: 3, title: 'Melle', firstName: 'Sophie', lastName: 'DUPONT', specialty: 'general practitioner', available: true },
]);
const compact = ref(false);

// the parent modifies ITS data: the children concerned update themselves
function toggleAvailability(): void {
  for (const m of doctors.value) {
    m.available = !m.available;
  }
}
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Example 07 - components and their props</h1>
    <div class="d-flex gap-3 mb-3">
      <label class="form-check-label"><input v-model="compact" type="checkbox" class="form-check-input"> compact display</label>
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" @click="toggleAvailability">Toggle availabilities</button>
    </div>
    <div class="row g-3">
      <div v-for="(m, i) in doctors" :key="m.id" class="col-md-4">
        <!-- :doctor="m" passes the OBJECT m (an expression);
             compact, without a colon, would pass the STRING "compact" -->
        <DoctorCard :doctor="m" :rank="i + 1" :compact="compact" />
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
  • line 14: in [<script setup>], an imported component is immediately usable in the template, like a new tag;
  • line 43: Each card receives ITS doctor. [:doctor="m"] (with a colon) passes the value of the expression [m]; without the colon, the character string ["m"] would be passed, which [TypeScript] would reject here. Component tag names are written as [PascalCase] to distinguish them from HTML tags;
  • lines 25–29: the parent modifies ITS data; the affected cards update.

The golden rule: a component never modifies its own props. Data flows from the parent to the child ([one-way data flow]): the parent owns it. To request a change, the child emits an event, which the parent processes: this is the subject of the following example.

docs.title: 3.2.1. Triggering an Event
docs.text:
The [Counter] component notifies its parent every time its button is clicked:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  08-component-events/src/components/Counter.vue
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  A child that NOTIFIES its parent: defineEmits declares the events
  it can emit, with the type of their data. The parent listens to them
  like HTML events: <Counter @change="..." @limit="...">.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue';

const props = defineProps<{ label: string; max: number }>();

// two events: 'change' (with the new value) and 'limit' (without data)
const emit = defineEmits<{
  change: [value: number];
  limit: [];
}>();

const value = ref(0);

function plus(): void {
  if (value.value >= props.max) {
    emit('limit');
    return;
  }
  value.value++;
  emit('change', value.value);
}
</script>

<template>
  <div class="d-flex align-items-center gap-2 mb-2">
    <span class="w-25">{{ label }}</span>
    <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" @click="plus">+1</button>
    <span class="badge text-bg-secondary">{{ value }} / {{ max }}</span>
  </div>
</template>
  • Lines 16–19: [defineEmits] declares the events that the component can trigger, along with their data types: [change] carries a number, [limit] carries nothing;
  • Lines 25 and 29: Emitting an event. [TypeScript] verifies the event name and its data type;
  • Line 21: The child is allowed to have its own state: [value] belongs to it, not to the parent.

docs.title: 3.2.2. v-model on a component
docs.text:
The component [TextField] is a “custom” form field: a label, the field itself, a tooltip, and a character counter. We want to use it with [v-model], just like a regular [<input>]:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  08-component-events/src/components/TextField.vue
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  A "home-made" form field (label + field + help + character
  counter) that accepts v-model, like an ordinary <input>:
      <TextField v-model="lastName" label="Last name" :max="20" />

  defineModel() creates a ref linked to the parent's v-model: READING it gives the
  parent's value, WRITING it emits the 'update:modelValue' event, which the
  parent handles by updating its data. The data thus remains
  the property of the parent.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useId } from 'vue';

const model = defineModel<string>({ required: true });
defineProps<{ label: string; max: number; help?: string }>();

// a unique identifier per instance, to link <label for> and <input id>
const id = useId();
</script>

<template>
  <div class="mb-3">
    <label class="form-label" :for="id">{{ label }}</label>
    <!-- v-model="model": the native field is linked to the ref of defineModel -->
    <input :id="id" v-model="model" class="form-control" :maxlength="max" :class="{ 'is-invalid': model.length === max }">
    <div class="form-text">{{ help }} ({{ model.length }} / {{ max }})</div>
  </div>
</template>
  • Line 18: [defineModel] creates a [ref] linked to the parent’s [v-model]. Reading it returns the parent’s value; writing to it triggers the [update:modelValue] event, which the parent handles by modifying ITS data. [v-model="lastName"] on a component is simply a shortcut for the [modelValue] property and this event: the data remains the property of the parent;
  • line 22: [useId()] provides a unique identifier per component instance: the two [TextField] instances on the page will not have the same [id], and each [<label for>] correctly refers to ITS field;
  • Line 29: The native field is linked to the [ref] from [defineModel].

docs.title: 3.2.3. The parent
docs.text:
<!--
  =========================================================================
  08-component-events/src/App.vue - the parent listens to its children
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Two ways for a child to pass information up:
    1. emitting an event, which the parent listens to with @ (Counter);
    2. v-model on a component (TextField): a shortcut for the prop
       modelValue + the event update:modelValue.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed, ref } from 'vue';
import Counter from './components/Counter.vue';
import TextField from './components/TextField.vue';

const total = ref(0);
const message = ref('');
const firstName = ref('Marie');
const lastName = ref('PELISSIER');
const fullName = computed(() => `${firstName.value} ${lastName.value.toUpperCase()}`);

// the handler of the 'change' event: it receives the emitted data
function onChange(label: string, value: number): void {
  total.value++;
  message.value = `${label} is now ${value}`;
}
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 640px">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Example 08 - events and v-model on a component</h1>

    <div class="card p-3 mb-4">
      <h2 class="h6">1. Events emitted by the children</h2>
      <Counter label="Coffees" :max="3" @change="(v) => onChange('Coffees', v)" @limit="message = 'No more than 3 coffees!'" />
      <Counter label="Glasses of water" :max="8" @change="(v) => onChange(`Glasses of water`, v)" @limit="message = 'Enough drinking.'" />
      <p class="mb-0">Total clicks: {{ total }} - <em>{{ message }}</em></p>
    </div>

    <div class="card p-3">
      <h2 class="h6">2. v-model on a component</h2>
      <TextField v-model="firstName" label="First name" :max="20" help="Required" />
      <TextField v-model="lastName" label="Last name" :max="20" help="Displayed in upper case" />
      <p class="mb-0">Data of the parent: <strong>{{ fullName }}</strong></p>
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary mt-2 align-self-start" @click="firstName = ''; lastName = ''">Clear (from the parent)</button>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
  • Line 35: The parent listens for events from its children using [@], just like HTML events. The arrowed function [(v) => onChange('Coffees', v)] receives the event data; [@limit] executes a single instruction;
  • line 42: [v-model] on a component;
  • line 45: when the PARENT empties its data, the fields follow: the link works both ways.

docs.title: 3.3. Example 09: Templates and Slots
docs.text:
Props pass data; slots pass content: from HTML, other components. The [Card] component sets the frame (border, header, footer), and its parent determines what goes inside it:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  09-slots/src/components/Card.vue - a reusable TEMPLATE
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Props pass DATA; slots pass CONTENT
  (HTML, other components). Card sets the frame (border, header,
  footer), the parent provides what goes inside:
    - <slot />              the default slot: the "main" content;
    - <slot name="header">  a named slot, filled by <template #header>;
    - the text placed BETWEEN <slot> and </slot> is displayed if the parent
      provides nothing (default content).
  It is the client-side equivalent of the layout.hbs template and its {{{body}}}
  in the NestJS course.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
defineProps<{ color?: 'primary' | 'success' | 'danger' }>();
</script>

<template>
  <div class="card mb-3" :class="color ? `border-${color}` : ''">
    <div class="card-header" :class="color ? `text-bg-${color}` : ''">
      <slot name="header">Untitled</slot>
    </div>
    <div class="card-body">
      <slot />
    </div>
    <!-- $slots.footer: did the parent provide a footer? If not, no empty <div> -->
    <div v-if="$slots.footer" class="card-footer text-muted small">
      <slot name="footer" />
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
  • line 23: a named slot; the text between [<slot>] and [</slot>] is displayed if the parent provides nothing;
  • line 26: the default slot: the “main” content;
  • line 29: [$slots] specifies which slots the parent has filled: without a footer, there is no empty [<div>].

This is the client-side equivalent of the [layout.hbs] template and its [{{{body}}}] in the [NestJS] course.

A second component, [DataTable], displays lines of any type:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  09-slots/src/components/DataTable.vue - a GENERIC table, with a "scoped" slot
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  generic="T": a generic component, like a generic TypeScript
  class - it displays rows of any type T.

  The table knows how to iterate over the rows, but not how to display a
  row: it PASSES each row to its slot (<slot name="row" :row="l">),
  and it is the parent that says what to do with it (<template #row="{ row }">).
  This is called a "scoped" slot: the content provided by the parent uses
  data that belongs to the child.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts" generic="T extends { id: number }">
defineProps<{ rows: T[]; columns: string[] }>();
</script>

<template>
  <table class="table table-sm align-middle mb-0">
    <thead>
      <tr><th v-for="c in columns" :key="c">{{ c }}</th></tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr v-for="(l, i) in rows" :key="l.id">
        <slot name="row" :row="l" :index="i" />
      </tr>
      <tr v-if="rows.length === 0">
        <td :colspan="columns.length" class="text-muted"><slot name="empty">No data.</slot></td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</template>
  • line 15: a generic component, such as a generic class [TypeScript]: [T] is the type of the lines, for which only one property is required: [id] (for the key of [v-for]);
  • Line 26: The array knows how to iterate through the lines, but not how to display a line. It passes each line to its slot, and the parent displays it. This is referred to as a “scoped” slot: the content provided by the parent uses data that belongs to the child.

The parent:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  09-slots/src/App.vue - using the Card and DataTable templates
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue';
import Card from './components/Card.vue';
import DataTable from './components/DataTable.vue';

interface Slot {
  id: number;
  time: string;
  patient: string | null;
}

const slots = ref<Slot[]>([
  { id: 1, time: '8:00 - 8:20', patient: null },
  { id: 2, time: '8:20 - 8:40', patient: 'Mme Alice DURAND' },
  { id: 3, time: '8:40 - 9:00', patient: null },
]);
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 720px">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Example 09 - templates and slots</h1>

    <!-- #header is the short form of v-slot:header -->
    <Card color="primary">
      <template #header>Schedule of Mme PELISSIER</template>
      <!-- the default slot: everything that is not in a <template #...> -->
      <DataTable :rows="slots" :columns="['#', 'Slot', 'Status']">
        <!-- we get the data passed by the DataTable: { row, index } -->
        <template #row="{ row, index }">
          <td>{{ index + 1 }}</td>
          <td>{{ row.time }}</td>
          <td>
            <span v-if="row.patient" class="badge text-bg-secondary">{{ row.patient }}</span>
            <span v-else class="badge text-bg-success">Free</span>
          </td>
        </template>
      </DataTable>
      <template #footer>{{ slots.filter((c) => c.patient === null).length }} free slot(s)</template>
    </Card>

    <Card color="success">
      <template #header>A card without a footer</template>
      <p class="mb-0">The footer is not provided: the card does not display it.</p>
    </Card>

    <Card>
      <!-- no header provided: the default content of the slot, "Untitled" -->
      <DataTable :rows="[]" :columns="['Name']">
        <template #empty>Nobody for now.</template>
      </DataTable>
    </Card>
  </div>
</template>
  • line 30: [<template #header>] (short for [v-slot:header]) fills the slot named [header];
  • line 32: anything not in a [<template #...>] goes into the default slot;
  • line 34: the data passed through the array is retrieved. Thanks to the generic component, [TypeScript] knows that [row] is a [Slot];
  • line 51: a card without a header: the default content, “Untitled,” is displayed.

docs.title: 3.4. Example 10: The Lifecycle of a Component
docs.text:
A component is created, displayed, updated, and then removed. [Vue.js] allows code to be executed at each of these stages. The [Clock] component:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  10-lifecycle/src/components/Clock.vue
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  The lifecycle of a component:
    1. setup      : the code of <script setup> runs (creation);
    2. onMounted  : the component is DISPLAYED, its HTML elements exist;
    3. onUpdated  : its display has just been updated;
    4. onUnmounted: the component has been REMOVED from the page.
  A clock starts a timer (setInterval) when displayed... and must
  absolutely stop it when it disappears: otherwise the timer
  would keep running for nothing (memory leak).
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { onMounted, onUnmounted, ref } from 'vue';

const emit = defineEmits<{ log: [message: string] }>();

const time = ref(new Date().toLocaleTimeString());
let timer: number | undefined;

emit('log', 'Clock: setup (creation)');

onMounted(() => {
  emit('log', 'Clock: onMounted - starting the timer');
  timer = window.setInterval(() => {
    time.value = new Date().toLocaleTimeString();
  }, 1000);
});

onUnmounted(() => {
  window.clearInterval(timer);
  emit('log', 'Clock: onUnmounted - timer stopped');
});
</script>

<template>
  <div class="display-6 font-monospace">{{ time }}</div>
</template>
  • line 23: the code for [<script setup>] runs once when the component is created;
  • lines 25–30: [onMounted]: the component is displayed, and its HTML elements exist. The timer is started;
  • lines 32–35: [onUnmounted]: the component has been removed from the page. The timer must be stopped; otherwise, it would continue to run for a component that no longer exists (a “memory leak”).

The parent:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  10-lifecycle/src/App.vue
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - v-if on <Clock>: checking / unchecking the box creates / destroys the
      component (onMounted / onUnmounted, see Clock.vue);
    - a "template ref": ref="field" gives access to the HTML <input> element
      itself, once the component is displayed (to give it the focus);
    - watch with { immediate: true }: executed right away, then on each
      change;
    - nextTick: waiting for Vue to have updated the page.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { nextTick, onMounted, ref, useTemplateRef, watch } from 'vue';
import Clock from './components/Clock.vue';

const withClock = ref(true);
const log = ref<string[]>([]);
const search = ref('');
const showSearch = ref(false);

// the <input ref="field"> element of the template (null as long as it is not displayed)
const field = useTemplateRef<HTMLInputElement>('field');

function trace(message: string): void {
  log.value.push(`${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()} ${message}`);
}

onMounted(() => trace('App: onMounted'));

watch(
  search,
  (value) => {
    document.title = value ? `Search: ${value}` : 'Example 10';
  },
  { immediate: true },
);

async function openSearch(): Promise<void> {
  showSearch.value = true;
  // at this moment, the <input> does not exist yet: Vue will update the page
  // a little later. nextTick() waits for this update.
  await nextTick();
  field.value?.focus();
}
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 720px">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Example 10 - the lifecycle of a component</h1>

    <div class="card p-3 mb-3">
      <label class="form-check-label mb-2">
        <input v-model="withClock" type="checkbox" class="form-check-input"> show the clock
      </label>
      <Clock v-if="withClock" @log="trace" />
    </div>

    <div class="card p-3 mb-3">
      <button v-if="!showSearch" class="btn btn-outline-primary align-self-start" @click="openSearch">
        Search...
      </button>
      <input v-else ref="field" v-model="search" class="form-control" placeholder="the tab title follows what you type">
    </div>

    <h2 class="h6">Log</h2>
    <ol class="small">
      <li v-for="(line, i) in log" :key="i">{{ line }}</li>
    </ol>
  </div>
</template>
  • Line 57: Checking and unchecking the box creates and destroys the clock: the log shows [setup], [onMounted], [onUnmounted];
  • Line 24: A template reference: The [ref="field"] attribute of the [<input>] element provides access to the HTML element itself. It is equal to [null] as long as the element is not displayed;
  • lines 32–37: [watch] with [{ immediate: true }] runs immediately, then on every change: the tab title updates as text is entered;
  • lines 40–45: After [showSearch.value = true], the field does not yet exist: [Vue.js] batches the page updates and performs them a little later. [await nextTick()] waits for this update; only then can focus be given to the field.

docs.title: 3.5. Example 11: Composables, provide, and inject
docs.text:
How can logic be shared between components? On the server side, [NestJS] had its services injected into the controllers. [Vue.js] has its composables: simple functions, whose names begin with [use], that combine reactive state and the accompanying code.

// =========================================================================
// 11-composables/src/composables/useClock.ts - a COMPOSABLE
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A composable is a simple function, whose name starts with "use"
// by convention, which groups a reactive state AND the logic that goes with it
// (here: the timer, its start and its stop). Every component that
// calls it gets ITS own clock, without copying the code.
//
// It is the Vue.js way of sharing logic between components - the
// role held, on the server side, by the NestJS services.
// =========================================================================

import { onMounted, onUnmounted, ref, type Ref } from 'vue';

export function useClock(periodMs = 1000): { now: Ref<Date> } {
  const now = ref(new Date());
  let timer: number | undefined;

  // the lifecycle hooks attach to the component that CALLS the composable
  onMounted(() => {
    timer = window.setInterval(() => (now.value = new Date()), periodMs);
  });
  onUnmounted(() => window.clearInterval(timer));

  return { now };
}
  • line 15: the function returns an object containing [ref] [now];
  • lines 20–22: The lifecycle functions called within a composable are attached to the component that calls the composable: each component has its own timer, which stops when the component is destroyed.

A second composable, without a lifecycle:

// =========================================================================
// 11-composables/src/composables/useCart.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A second composable, WITHOUT lifecycle: a cart (list of items,
// total, adding, removing). Each call of useCart() creates a NEW
// cart: two components that call it each have their own.
// (For a cart SHARED by the whole application, see provide / inject
// below, and Pinia in example 15.)
// =========================================================================

import { computed, ref } from 'vue';

export interface Item {
  label: string;
  price: number;
}

export function useCart() {
  const items = ref<Item[]>([]);
  const total = computed(() => items.value.reduce((sum, a) => sum + a.price, 0));

  function add(item: Item): void {
    items.value.push(item);
  }
  function remove(index: number): void {
    items.value.splice(index, 1);
  }

  return { items, total, add, remove };
}

// the type of what useCart returns: useful for provide / inject
export type Cart = ReturnType<typeof useCart>;
  • line 19: each call to [useCart()] creates a NEW shopping cart;
  • line 33: the type of what [useCart] returns, inferred by [TypeScript].

To allow multiple components to share the SAME shopping cart, we use [provide] and [inject], a form of dependency injection:

// =========================================================================
// 11-composables/src/keys.ts - the keys of provide / inject
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// provide(key, value): a component MAKES AVAILABLE a value for
// all its descendants, whatever their depth;
// inject(key): a descendant retrieves it - without the intermediate
// components having to pass it from props to props.
// It is a form of dependency injection, as in NestJS.
//
// An InjectionKey<T> (a typed Symbol) guarantees that inject() returns a
// value of the right type.
// =========================================================================

import type { InjectionKey } from 'vue';
import type { Cart } from './composables/useCart';

export const CART_KEY: InjectionKey<Cart> = Symbol('cart');
  • Line 17: the key under which the shopping cart is provided: a [Symbol] (unique value) typed by [InjectionKey<Cart>], so that [inject] returns an object of the correct type.

The root component creates the shopping cart and provides it:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  11-composables/src/App.vue
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    - useClock(): App has its clock (1 s), CartSummary its own (5 s);
    - useCart() + provide: App creates ONE cart and provides it to all its
      descendants; Catalog and CartSummary inject it and therefore
      share the same one.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { provide } from 'vue';
import { useClock } from './composables/useClock';
import { useCart } from './composables/useCart';
import { CART_KEY } from './keys';
import Catalog from './components/Catalog.vue';
import CartSummary from './components/CartSummary.vue';

const { now } = useClock();
provide(CART_KEY, useCart());
</script>

<template>
  <div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 720px">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Example 11 - composables and provide / inject</h1>
    <p class="text-muted">Clock of App: {{ now.toLocaleTimeString() }}</p>
    <div class="row g-3">
      <div class="col-md-6"><Catalog /></div>
      <div class="col-md-6"><CartSummary /></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
  • line 19: App has its own clock, refreshed every second;
  • line 20: The app makes a shopping cart available to ALL its descendants, regardless of their depth, without having to pass it from props to props.

Two descendants inject it:

<!--
  11-composables/src/components/Catalog.vue - a descendant that INJECTS the cart
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { inject } from 'vue';
import { CART_KEY } from '../keys';
import type { Item } from '../composables/useCart';

// the cart provided by App.vue (provide); explicit error if it is missing
const cart = inject(CART_KEY);
if (!cart) {
  throw new Error('Catalog must be placed under a component that provides the cart');
}

const catalog: Item[] = [
  { label: 'Consultation', price: 30 },
  { label: 'Vaccine', price: 12.5 },
  { label: 'Certificate', price: 5 },
];
</script>

<template>
  <ul class="list-group">
    <li v-for="a in catalog" :key="a.label" class="list-group-item d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center">
      {{ a.label }} (€{{ a.price }})
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" @click="cart.add(a)">Add</button>
    </li>
  </ul>
</template>
  • line 10: The basket provided by an ancestor is retrieved; [inject] returns [undefined] if no ancestor has provided it: this is indicated by an explicit error.
<!--
  11-composables/src/components/CartSummary.vue - another descendant, the SAME cart
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { inject } from 'vue';
import { CART_KEY } from '../keys';
import { useClock } from '../composables/useClock';

const cart = inject(CART_KEY)!;
// this component has ITS own clock, refreshed every 5 seconds
const { now } = useClock(5000);
</script>

<!-- cart.items.value: in a template, Vue only "unwraps" (implicit
     .value) the TOP-LEVEL refs of the script, like now.
     The refs stored INSIDE an object (cart.items) are written with .value -->
<template>
  <div class="card p-3">
    <h2 class="h6">Cart ({{ cart.items.value.length }} item(s)) - {{ now.toLocaleTimeString() }}</h2>
    <ul class="mb-2">
      <li v-for="(a, i) in cart.items.value" :key="i">
        {{ a.label }} <a href="#" @click.prevent="cart.remove(i)">remove</a>
      </li>
    </ul>
    <strong>Total: €{{ cart.total.value }}</strong>
  </div>
</template>
  • Line 9: Same injection; [!] confirms to [TypeScript] that the value exists;
  • line 11: this component has its OWN clock, refreshed every 5 seconds;
  • line 19: in a template, [Vue.js] automatically “unpacks” only the top-level [ref] elements of the script. A [ref] stored INSIDE an object ([cart.items]) is written with [.value].

Both components display the same shopping cart; the two clocks run at their own pace:

docs.title: 3.6. Example 12: A Reusable Confirmation Window
docs.text:
Before deleting an item, the system asks, “Are you sure?” The browser function [window.confirm()] exists, but its dialog box cannot be formatted, nor can its buttons be translated. We replace it with a [Bootstrap] window, controlled by a composable. This is the [Vue.js] version of Example 21 from the [NestJS] course.

// =========================================================================
// 12-confirmation/src/composables/useConfirmation.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// "Are you sure?": window.confirm() exists, but it can neither be
// styled, nor can its buttons be translated. We replace it with a Bootstrap
// dialog (ConfirmDialog.vue), driven by this composable.
//
// The trick: confirm(message) returns a PROMISE, resolved to true (Yes)
// or false (No) when the user answers. The calling code is then written
// as simply as with window.confirm:
//
//     if (await confirm('Delete this doctor?')) { ... }
//
// The state (displayed message, function to call on the answer) is declared
// OUTSIDE the function: it is therefore UNIQUE for the whole application. A
// single dialog, placed once in App.vue, serves all the components.
// =========================================================================

import { readonly, ref } from 'vue';

const message = ref<string | null>(null); // null: dialog closed
let answer: ((yes: boolean) => void) | null = null;

export function useConfirmation() {
  function confirm(text: string): Promise<boolean> {
    message.value = text;
    return new Promise<boolean>((resolve) => {
      answer = resolve;
    });
  }

  function respond(yes: boolean): void {
    message.value = null;
    answer?.(yes);
    answer = null;
  }

  // readonly: the components read the message, only the composable modifies it
  return { message: readonly(message), confirm, respond };
}
  • Lines 21 and 22: The state is declared OUTSIDE the function [useConfirmation] at the module level. It is therefore unique across the entire application: a single window serves all components;
  • Lines 25–30: [confirm] opens the window (by assigning a value to the message) and returns a promise. It stores the function [resolve] from this promise in [answer]: the promise will not be resolved until the user has responded;
  • lines 32–35: The user’s response closes the window and resolves the promise to [true] or [false];
  • line 39: components can read the message, but not modify it.

The window:

<!--
  =========================================================================
  12-confirmation/src/components/ConfirmDialog.vue
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  The modal dialog, placed ONCE in App.vue.
    - <Teleport to="body">: its HTML is inserted at the end of <body>, outside
      the component tree - a modal dialog must go
      above everything, wherever it is declared;
    - same Bootstrap classes as a real modal (.modal, .modal-backdrop),
      displayed "hard-coded" (show d-block): no need for Bootstrap's JavaScript;
    - keyboard: Escape = No; the focus is placed on the "No" button (the
      least dangerous choice) on opening.
  =========================================================================
-->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { nextTick, onUnmounted, useTemplateRef, watch } from 'vue';
import { useConfirmation } from '../composables/useConfirmation';

const { message, respond } = useConfirmation();
const noButton = useTemplateRef<HTMLButtonElement>('noButton');

function onKeydown(e: KeyboardEvent): void {
  if (e.key === 'Escape') {
    respond(false);
  }
}

// on opening: focus on "No", listening to the Escape key; on closing: we stop listening
watch(message, async (value) => {
  if (value !== null) {
    document.addEventListener('keydown', onKeydown);
    await nextTick();
    noButton.value?.focus();
